Sen's stated use is timely video of environmental events and natural disasters such as wildfires, floods and storms.

EUTE.purpose: A Eutelsat geostationary satellite. Eutelsat, headquartered in Paris, runs one of Europe's two large commercial GEO fleets, carrying television distribution — the HOT BIRD neighbourhood at 13° East is its flagship broadcast position — alongside Ka-band broadband under the KONNECT name and mobility capacity for aircraft and ships. Since the 2023 combination with OneWeb the company operates in both geostationary and low Earth orbit, which is unusual: most operators have one or the other. The registry abbreviates the operator name to EUTE in most of these entries, so the published spacecraft names do not all read as "Eutelsat".

EUTELSAT.purpose: A Eutelsat geostationary satellite. Eutelsat, headquartered in Paris, runs one of Europe's two large commercial GEO fleets, carrying television distribution alongside Ka-band broadband under the KONNECT name and mobility capacity for aircraft and ships; since the 2023 combination with OneWeb it operates in both geostationary and low Earth orbit. This entry exists separately from the EUTE one because the registry spells the operator two different ways across the same fleet — a difference that has silently broken name-matching rules on this site before.

EUTELSAT KA-SAT.purpose: KA-SAT was Europe's first large Ka-band high-throughput satellite, launched in 2010 with eighty-two spot beams for consumer broadband, and its ground network was operated by Viasat. It is also the object lesson every SATCOM planner should know: at 04:45 UTC on 24 February 2022, an hour before Russian forces crossed into Ukraine, an attacker reached the KA-SAT management network and pushed wiper malware that bricked tens of thousands of consumer modems across Ukraine and the rest of Europe. Nothing was wrong with the spacecraft. The attack went through the ground segment — which is where satellite communications are usually attacked.

EXACTVIEW-1.purpose: A dedicated space-based AIS receiver, built on an SSTL bus with a second-generation AIS payload from COM DEV, flown for exactEarth of Cambridge, Ontario. AIS transponders are mandated by the IMO on vessels over 300 tons, but the signal is line-of-sight and shore stations only see about 50 km out; a receiver in orbit turns that into ocean-basin coverage, which is the whole point for anyone tracking shipping beyond the littoral. Its payload was designed specifically to improve detection in dense traffic, where overlapping AIS bursts collide. The spacecraft was sold to Myriota in 2020 to seed that company's IoT service.

EXO-0.purpose: EXO-0 is an 8U cubesat built by EnduroSat and notable for how it got where it is: it was the first satellite Exotrail released from a spacevan orbital transfer vehicle, on 28 February 2024, which made Exotrail a space-services provider rather than only a propulsion supplier. The demonstration matters more than the spacecraft — it established that a commercial tug can take a rideshare passenger from the drop-off orbit to a different one and deploy it there.

EYCORE-1.purpose: Eycore-1 is the first Polish satellite carrying a domestically developed synthetic aperture radar, an X-band system with a deployable active phased-array antenna flown on a Kongsberg NanoAvionics MP42 microsatellite bus. Eycore is a subsidiary of Advanced Protection Systems, a maker of military counter-drone systems, and the satellite is explicitly dual-use: all-weather, day-and-night imaging aimed at intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance for European and NATO users as well as civil tasking. The launch also advances Poland's POLSARIS military radar constellation.

FALCON EYE 2.purpose: A high-resolution optical reconnaissance satellite owned and operated by the United Arab Emirates, built by Airbus Defence and Space with Thales Alenia Space supplying the optical instrument and the image processing chain. Airbus states plainly that the FalconEye system supports the needs of the UAE's Armed Forces. It is the surviving half of a two-satellite system, its sister spacecraft having been lost in a launch failure.

FARADAY PHOENIX.purpose: A 6U hosted-payload satellite from In-Space Missions of the UK, developed in under eight months and flown as what the company calls the world's first commercial rideshare satellite mission - a rideshare within a rideshare, carrying payloads for six separate customers including Airbus, Lacuna, SatixFy and Aeternum. Its own Babel payload is a high-gain wideband software-defined radio with over 500 MHz of bandwidth whose applications can be uploaded in orbit; In-Space cites tracking ship radars among them, which is the RF-collection thread that leads on to the company's Azalea cluster.

FFI ARCSAT.purpose: ARCSAT is a Norwegian Defence Research Establishment demonstration of military UHF tactical communications relayed through a small satellite in polar low Earth orbit. UHF tactical satellite is the band a dismounted or small-boat user can work with a manpack radio and a simple antenna, and the American and NATO UHF constellations are geostationary — which means they are unusable at the latitudes Norway cares most about. A polar relay is the obvious answer, and this mission is the experiment that tests whether a cheap one is good enough.

FGN-100-D.purpose: Demonstrators for the positioning-satellite constellation being built by Fergani Space, the Turkish company founded by Baykar chairman Selcuk Bayraktar. Fergani describes FGN-100-D2 as its second fully indigenous satellite and, at 104 kg, the largest satellite built by a Turkish private company; the line tests domestically developed avionics with a triple-redundant flight computer, green propulsion, telemetry and telecommand links and payload communications. The declared end state is a Turkish-owned positioning constellation, which if fielded would be a sovereign alternative to foreign PNT for Turkish users.

FIREFLY.purpose: Pixxel's Firefly hyperspectral constellation. Each satellite images in hundreds of narrow spectral bands at about 5 m ground resolution -- roughly six times sharper than the 30 m that had been standard for hyperspectral instruments -- which is what moves the technique from landscape scale to field scale: crop disease, methane and other gas plumes, mineral signatures and water quality. Pixxel is a private operator founded in India, not an ISRO programme, and the first Fireflies were the opening tranche of a constellation still being built out.

FORESAIL.organization: Finnish Centre of Excellence in Sustainable Space / Aalto University
FORESAIL.purpose: A Foresail cubesat, built at Aalto University for the Finnish Centre of Excellence in Sustainable Space. It carries PATE, a particle telescope from the University of Turku that measures the energies and pitch angles of electrons from roughly 80 to 1600 keV and of protons — in other words, it measures the radiation belt population that governs internal charging and single-event upsets in every other satellite in that region. It also flies a plasma-brake deorbit device from the Finnish Meteorological Institute, so the mission tests both a space-weather instrument and a way of not becoming debris.

FORGESTAR-1.purpose: The UK's first in-space manufacturing satellite, designed, built and qualified in Cardiff by Space Forge, and the first UK spacecraft to receive an in-space manufacturing licence from the Civil Aviation Authority. Its purpose is to grow high-performance semiconductor materials - gallium nitride, silicon carbide, aluminium nitride, diamond - in the vacuum and microgravity of orbit, and in late 2025 it generated plasma in its onboard growth chamber more than a hundred times, which Space Forge describes as the first time a commercial free-flying spacecraft has demonstrated the conditions needed for gas-phase crystal growth. The company also intends to validate re-entry technology to bring the material home.

FORMOSAT-5 TAIWAN.purpose: The third flight unit of Taiwan's FORMOSAT programme and the first remote-sensing satellite Taiwan designed and built itself, including the optical instrument. Its main mission is high-resolution land observation for mapping, agriculture and disaster assessment, and the World Meteorological Organization also records it as a significant contributor to space-weather observation through its secondary science payload.

FORMOSAT-8A.purpose: The first satellite of Taiwan's FORMOSAT-8 optical constellation, named the Chi Po-lin Satellite after the documentary film-maker who photographed Taiwan from the air. Eight are planned; each returns about 1 m ground detail, sharpened to roughly 0.7 m in processing, and TASA states the constellation exists to address the natural disasters and security risks Taiwan faces.

FOSSASat-2E.purpose: A FOSSASat-2E spacecraft from the Madrid company FOSSA Systems, which builds very small nano- and picosatellites in numbers rather than a few large ones and flies them as a connectivity constellation. FOSSA describes the FOSSASat generation as delivering secure connectivity - satellite Internet of Things, and RF payloads up to signals intelligence - from low orbit, closing the gap between remote assets and the people who need to monitor and control them beyond terrestrial network coverage. In practice these units relay short low-rate telemetry from fixed and mobile assets in places with no ground network at all, which is the same operational problem a deployed unit or a vessel outside coverage has.

FRAUNHOFER ERNST.purpose: ERNST is a 12U cubesat built by the Fraunhofer Institute for High-Speed Dynamics and the first small satellite mission flown for the German armed forces. It carries a cryogenically cooled infrared imager, and its purpose is to test whether a spacecraft this small can do early missile detection — a job that has always required large, expensive satellites in high orbits. After a year on orbit Fraunhofer reported that it had imaged rockets during launch, tracking a Falcon 9 in the infrared for nearly three minutes to upper-stage separation. It is a demonstrator, not an operational warning asset, and Fraunhofer describes it as such.

FUNCUBE 1.purpose: AMSAT-UK's first CubeSat, also designated AMSAT-OSCAR 73, built for educational outreach and for radio amateurs. It carries a 145.935 MHz BPSK telemetry beacon that schools can receive with a low-cost USB dongle receiver, plus an inverting SSB/CW linear transponder with a 435 MHz uplink and 145 MHz downlink that is usually enabled on night passes and at weekends. A materials-science experiment onboard lets pupils compare telemetry against the same experiment run in a classroom.

GARAI-A.purpose: GARAI-A is Satlantis's first submetre-class microsatellite, flown on an OHB Sweden InnoSat platform with two double-channel Satlantis instruments, iSIM-90 and the larger iSIM-170, combining multispectral and shortwave-infrared imaging with a polarimetry channel and video. It is the forerunner of the Atlantic Constellation, the Iberian partnership between Satlantis, Portugal's GEOSAT and CEiiA, and its stated applications include coastal and border awareness alongside infrastructure and food-security monitoring.

GCOM-C SHIKISAI.purpose: Shikisai, the climate half of JAXA's Global Change Observation Mission. Its Second-generation Global Imager observes 19 bands from the near ultraviolet to the thermal infrared, yielding cloud, aerosol, ocean colour, sea and land surface temperature, snow and ice, and vegetation products tied to the carbon cycle and the Earth's radiation budget. Ocean colour and sea-surface temperature from this class of imager are the standard inputs to coastal water-clarity and frontal analysis.

GCOM-W1 SHIZUKU.purpose: Shizuku, the water-cycle half of JAXA's Global Change Observation Mission. Its single instrument, the AMSR2 passive microwave radiometer, sweeps a 1450 km swath and returns global precipitation, ocean surface wind speed, water vapour, sea-ice concentration and soil moisture. Those are core METOC fields: microwave radiometry sees through cloud, so AMSR2 products feed sea-ice edge and sea-surface analyses that optical sensors cannot deliver in bad weather.

GEISAT PRECURSOR.purpose: GEISAT Precursor is a 16U CubeSat from the Bilbao company Satlantis, its first end-to-end mission, built around the company's iSIM-90 imager. One optical channel covers the visible and near infrared at about 2 m ground sampling and a second covers the shortwave infrared at about 5 m; the pairing is what allows methane plumes to be detected and quantified by multispectral differential photometry. The mission has been selected as a Copernicus Contributing Mission for greenhouse-gas work.

GESAT GEN 1.purpose: GESat GEN1 is the pathfinder for Absolut Sensing's planned sixteen-satellite methane-monitoring constellation. It measures methane concentration and emission rate at the scale of an individual facility, with the ability to be retasked quickly onto a suspected source as well as to map broadly, and this first spacecraft exists to validate both the instrument concept and the ground processing chain before the constellation is committed.

GLOBALSTAR.purpose: A Globalstar second-generation satellite, part of a low-Earth-orbit mobile-satellite constellation flying at about 1,410 km and 52° inclination. Globalstar spacecraft are deliberately simple bent pipes: they carry no inter-satellite links and no onboard switching, so a call only works when the handset and a ground gateway are visible to the same satellite at the same moment. That design choice is why coverage is good over populated land masses and poor in mid-ocean and at high latitude, and it also makes the network cheap enough to serve very low-rate traffic — the constellation carries Apple's Emergency SOS via satellite for iPhone, funded by a $450 million Apple investment in Globalstar ground infrastructure.

GOKTURK 2.organization: Turkish Ministry of National Defence / TUBITAK UZAY
GOKTURK 2.purpose: Turkiye's first high-resolution Earth observation satellite, built in-country by TUBITAK UZAY and Turkish Aerospace under a contract signed with the Ministry of National Defence. TUBITAK UZAY publishes its imaging performance as 2.5 m panchromatic and 5 m colour from about 686 km, which places it in the dual-use reconnaissance class rather than the sub-metre class. It is operated as a national imaging asset serving both defence and civil users, and it was the programme that first proved Turkish design, integration and test capability for an operational imaging spacecraft.

GOKTURK-1A.assessedBy: Turkish Aerospace (TUSAS), the programme's Turkish industrial participant
GOKTURK-1A.purpose: Turkiye's very-high-resolution optical reconnaissance satellite, procured by the Presidency of Defence Industries with Telespazio as prime contractor and Thales Alenia Space France as main subcontractor, and with Turkish Aerospace supplying flight structure and taking part in the work packages. Turkish Aerospace describes the system as enabling high-resolution imagery of any region on Earth without geographical restriction, for both military and civil applications. The camera's actual ground resolution and the tasking arrangements are not published, so treat any specific figure you see with caution.

GOMX 1.purpose: GOMX-1, renamed GATOSS after launch, is a 2U cubesat flown by GomSpace — an Aalborg University spin-out — to demonstrate that aircraft ADS-B transponder signals can be received from orbit. ADS-B is line-of-sight and so is invisible to ground receivers over ocean and polar routes, which is the coverage gap that space-based reception fills; the same argument that later produced operational aircraft-tracking constellations was being tested here on a satellite the size of a milk carton.

GOSAT IBUKI GHG.organization: JAXA / NIES / Ministry of the Environment
GOSAT IBUKI GHG.purpose: Ibuki, the world's first spacecraft built to measure carbon dioxide and methane concentrations from space, flown jointly by JAXA, the National Institute for Environmental Studies and Japan's Ministry of the Environment. Its TANSO instrument pairs a Fourier transform spectrometer, which reads the absorption signature of the two gases in reflected sunlight and thermal emission, with a cloud and aerosol imager used to screen contaminated soundings.

GOSAT-2 IBUKI-2.organization: JAXA / NIES / Ministry of the Environment
GOSAT-2 IBUKI-2.purpose: Ibuki-2, the follow-on greenhouse-gas observatory. Its FTS-2 spectrometer covers wider spectral regions than GOSAT or NASA's OCO-2 and so retrieves methane, water vapour and carbon monoxide in addition to carbon dioxide, the carbon monoxide channel making it possible to separate combustion sources from other emissions. A pointing system steers the instrument around cloud in real time to raise the yield of clear soundings.

GOSAT-GW IBUKI GW.organization: JAXA / NIES / Ministry of the Environment
GOSAT-GW IBUKI GW.purpose: Ibuki GW, the Global Observing Satellite for Greenhouse gases and Water cycle, which merges two Japanese observing lines onto one spacecraft. It carries TANSO-3, the next greenhouse-gas spectrometer, together with AMSR3, the successor to the AMSR2 microwave radiometer flown on GCOM-W1, so continuity of the sea-surface temperature, ocean wind, water vapour and sea-ice record depends on this satellite.

GRAY JAY (JAY-C / JAY-D).assessedBy: Gunter's Space Page and SpaceQ, reporting the DRDC programme
GRAY JAY (JAY-C / JAY-D).purpose: The Gray Jay constellation: three ~30 kg microsatellites built by the UTIAS Space Flight Laboratory on the DEFIANT bus for Defence Research and Development Canada, the science and technology arm of the Department of National Defence. They fly in close formation to demonstrate multi-sensor detection and identification of surface or airborne targets in Canada's Arctic, under the All-Domain Situational Awareness programme, building directly on the CanX-4/CanX-5 formation-flying result. The sensor complement has not been published in detail; the declared purpose is remote surveillance and situational awareness of the Arctic approaches.

GRUS.purpose: A GRUS microsatellite of AxelGlobe, the commercial Earth-observation constellation Axelspace runs from Tokyo. Each is a 100 kg-class optical imager returning 2.5 m multispectral imagery, and the whole point of the design is fleet economics: enough cheap satellites that a customer gets a fresh look at a site every few days instead of queueing for time on one large spacecraft. Axelspace sells the imagery for agriculture, forestry, mapping and infrastructure monitoring.

GRUS-1A.purpose: The first satellite of GRUS, the roughly 100 kg microsatellite line built by the Japanese company Axelspace as the building block of its AxelGlobe Earth observation constellation, delivering about 2.5 m ground resolution. GRUS-1A entered normal operations in 2019 and AxelGlobe began commercial service that May, with the constellation intended to monitor the planet's land surface at high revisit. It is catalogued here without a settled registry attribution, but the operator and mission are documented by the company.

GRUS-3 NEXT GENERATION.purpose: One of the seven next-generation GRUS-3 optical microsatellites Axelspace launched together to enlarge its AxelGlobe constellation past the original five GRUS-1 spacecraft. Axelspace's stated aim for the expansion is observation of broader areas at higher frequency, serving precision agriculture, forest monitoring and map creation alongside environmental, financial and property analytics.

GRUS-3ALPHA PRECURSOR.purpose: GRUS-3 alpha, the precursor Axelspace flew a year ahead of its GRUS-3 constellation. It carries the optical system, telescope and detector, intended for the operational GRUS-3 satellites, and exists to prove that hardware and the satellite bus in orbit before the production run was committed. It is a validation spacecraft, not a member of the imaging service.

GSAT.purpose: India's operational geostationary communications series, flown as part of the INSAT system that ISRO calls one of the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the Asia-Pacific. Between them the INSAT/GSAT spacecraft carry more than 200 transponders in C, extended C and Ku band and supply telecommunications, television broadcasting, satellite newsgathering, weather forecasting support, disaster warning and search-and-rescue relay. Individual members differ sharply -- several are dedicated military or navigation-augmentation spacecraft -- so which GSAT you are looking at matters more than the series name.

GSAT 11.purpose: ISRO's first heavy multi-spot-beam broadband satellite and the heaviest spacecraft the agency has built, described by ISRO as the fore-runner of a series of advanced communications satellites with multi-spot beam antenna coverage over the Indian mainland and islands. Multi-spot beam design is what lets one satellite reuse the same spectrum many times over and push broadband to small terminals, including on outlying island territory.

GSAT 19.purpose: A Ka/Ku-band high-throughput communications satellite, and the first spacecraft launched by India's GSLV Mk III. Alongside the transponders it carries the Geostationary Radiation Spectrometer, which monitors charged particles and the influence of space radiation on satellites and their electronic components -- a space-weather instrument riding on an operational comsat, measuring the environment that determines how long everything else in that orbit survives.

GSAT 20 (GSAT-N2).purpose: Marketed as GSAT-N2, this is NewSpace India Limited's demand-driven high-throughput satellite: Ka-band, about 48 Gbps of capacity and 32 spot beams giving nationwide coverage including the Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands. Its declared job is broadband and in-flight connectivity across India, which is the maritime and aviation mobility market rather than broadcasting. It was built by ISRO's UR Rao Satellite Centre for NSIL, the Department of Space's commercial arm.

GSAT 29.purpose: A multi-beam, multiband high-throughput satellite carrying Ka and Ku-band transponders aimed at users in Jammu and Kashmir and the North Eastern regions of India. It is also ISRO's testbed for what comes after Ka-band: a Q/V-band technology demonstration payload, a geostationary high-resolution camera, and the agency's first use of an optical communications payload for data transmission.

GSAT 30.purpose: A C and Ku-band replacement for the ageing INSAT-4A, built on ISRO's enhanced I-3K bus. Its Ku-band beam covers the Indian mainland and islands while the C-band beam reaches far beyond national territory -- ISRO's own description extends it over the Gulf countries, a large number of Asian countries and Australia. That makes it one of the wider-footprint Indian civil comsats over the northern Indian Ocean.

GSAT 6.purpose: A geostationary communications satellite whose distinguishing feature is a six-metre S-band unfurlable antenna -- the largest satellite antenna ISRO had built -- feeding five S-band spot beams over the Indian mainland, with a single C-band beam at the hub end of the link. A large reflector, small user terminals and frequency reuse between spot beams is the signature of a mobile satellite communications payload rather than a broadcast one.

GSAT 7 (RUKMINI).purpose: India's dedicated naval communications satellite, known in service as Rukmini. ISRO states that the payload is designed to provide communication capabilities to users over a wide oceanic region including the Indian land-mass, with a multiband design spanning low bit-rate voice through to high bit-rate data. That is a blue-water SATCOM footprint rather than a landmass one: it is what allows the Indian Navy to hold ships, submarines and maritime patrol aircraft on a national network far out into the Indian Ocean instead of leasing foreign mobile-satellite capacity.

GSAT 7A.purpose: The air-arm counterpart to the Navy's GSAT-7. ISRO publishes only that GSAT-7A is built on its I-2K bus to provide communication capability in Ku-band over the Indian region; Gunter's Space Page records it as a communications satellite for shared use of the Indian Air Force and the Indian Army, with a switchable Ku-band frequency plan for mobile users, one Gregorian reflector and four steerable antennas. That configuration fits the stated purpose of linking dispersed airbases, ground radars and airborne early warning aircraft, but the user assignment is assessed rather than officially declared.

GSAT 9 (SOUTH ASIA SATELLITE).purpose: The South Asia Satellite: a Ku-band geostationary communications spacecraft India built and operates as a regional instrument rather than a purely national one. ISRO gives its primary objective as providing various communication applications in Ku-band with coverage over South Asian countries, and the satellite was offered to neighbouring states for telecommunications, broadcasting and disaster communications. The bus is the same standard I-2K used by India's other mid-size comsats, so what distinguishes GSAT-9 is its footprint and its politics, not its hardware.

GSAT GAGAN PAYLOAD CARRIERS.purpose: Three of India's Ku-band communications satellites double as the space segment of GAGAN, the GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation system, broadcasting in the L1 and L5 bands. GAGAN is India's satellite-based augmentation system: it transmits GPS corrections and integrity messages so that civil aviation and other precision users over the Indian region get better accuracy and, more importantly, a prompt warning when a GPS signal should not be trusted. ISRO records GSAT-15 as the third satellite to carry the GAGAN payload after GSAT-8 and GSAT-10, which were already providing navigation services from orbit.

GXIBA-1.organization: Universidad Popular Autonoma del Estado de Puebla
GXIBA-1.purpose: A 1U CubeSat built by students and staff at the Popular Autonomous University of the State of Puebla and deployed from the International Space Station in February 2026 under the UNOOSA-JAXA KiboCUBE programme. Its mission is to photograph Mexico's active volcanoes in the visible spectrum, chiefly Popocatepetl, and to deliver ash-dispersion analysis to CENAPRED, the national disaster prevention centre. Volcanic ash is an aviation hazard, so the product has a direct operational consumer even at CubeSat quality.

GYEONGGISAT-1.purpose: Korea's first climate satellite commissioned by a local government, built and operated by Nara Space Technology for Gyeonggi Province. Its optical multispectral camera collects visible and near-infrared imagery, which the province buys as working data for disaster monitoring, urban change detection and rice-crop analysis. Two follow-on spacecraft tuned to greenhouse gases, methane in particular, are planned behind it.

HAMMER.purpose: HAMMER stands for Hyperspectral AI for Marine Monitoring and Emergency Response, an in-orbit demonstration satellite built by Open Cosmos with the UK Satellite Applications Catapult. It carries a miniaturised hyperspectral imager alongside two Ubotica AI processing boards, so scenes are analysed on board and only the useful product is downlinked, and an inter-satellite link that lets data hop to another spacecraft rather than waiting for a ground-station pass. The declared operational target is Atlantic coastal and high-seas monitoring with near-real-time detection of illegal fishing.

HEINRICH HERTZ H2SAT.purpose: Heinrich Hertz, catalogued as H2Sat, is a German geostationary communications satellite flown to qualify new communications technology in orbit — around twenty experiments in payload, antenna and onboard-processing hardware, run by DLR with the German space industry. It also carries a separate communications payload for the Bundeswehr, which is what makes it a dual-purpose spacecraft rather than a pure technology mission: Germany gets flight heritage for its industry and additional military capacity from the same launch.

HELLAS-SAT 3.purpose: Hellas-Sat 3 is a condominium spacecraft at 39° East: one satellite carrying two owners' payloads. The Ku-band mission belongs to Hellas Sat, an Arabsat subsidiary, and replaced Hellas-Sat 2's direct-to-home and telecom services across Europe, the Middle East and southern Africa with more than double the transponder count; the S-band payload belongs to Inmarsat and is the space segment of the European Aviation Network. Shared spacecraft like this are common at contested orbital slots, and they are the reason a single catalogue number can have two operators with two entirely different missions.

HERMES Pathfinder.purpose: A HERMES Pathfinder nanosatellite: six 3U CubeSats flown as a distributed X-ray and gamma-ray observatory, coordinated by Italy's National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) with ASI, three units funded by ASI and three under the EU Horizon 2020 HERMES-SP project. Each carries a miniaturised detector pairing GAGG scintillator crystals with silicon drift detectors - the 'siswich' design - sensitive from about 2 keV to 2 MeV with sub-microsecond timing. Because the payload has no imaging optics, the constellation locates gamma-ray bursts by triangulating the arrival-time differences of the same burst across at least three spacecraft, which also makes it a fast localiser for the electromagnetic counterparts of gravitational-wave events.

HIBARI VSAC.purpose: HIBARI, a 50 kg demonstration satellite from the Tokyo Institute of Technology flown as a theme on JAXA's second Innovative Satellite Technology Demonstration mission. It tests variable-shape attitude control: four movable solar paddles are swung to change the spacecraft's own moment of inertia and slew it quickly, instead of relying only on reaction wheels. Fast slewing is what lets a small imaging satellite take several targets on one pass.

HMU-SAT2 TERUTERU.purpose: HMU-SAT2, nicknamed Teruteru after the paper dolls Japanese children hang up to wish for fine weather. It is an education and technology-demonstration nanosatellite developed jointly by the Hokkaido University of Science, the firm Koubou Okura and Komagane Technical High School, and its payload is a bank of light-emitting diodes that flash Morse code to observers on the ground.

HODOYOSHI.purpose: A Hodoyoshi microsatellite, developed by the University of Tokyo with NESTRA under Japan's FIRST research programme. The name means reasonably reliable, and that was the thesis: design 50 kg-class satellites to a sensible rather than exhaustive reliability standard so they can be mass-produced cheaply. Both carry optical imagers, Hodoyoshi-3 at low and medium resolution and Hodoyoshi-4 at 6 to 10 m, plus a store-and-forward payload that collects data from remote ground sensors.

HORACIO.purpose: HORACIO is Satlantis's third full end-to-end Earth-observation satellite, a 16U CubeSat carrying the company's iSIM-90 high-resolution optical instrument with simultaneous visible/near-infrared and shortwave-infrared channels and a highly agile pointing design. Satlantis markets it for infrastructure monitoring, methane quantification and food security, and explicitly for coastal and border awareness.

HORIZONS SATELLITE.purpose: A Horizons satellite, owned by the joint venture Intelsat and Japan's SKY Perfect JSAT formed in 2001 to serve the Pacific between them. Horizons 3e sits at 169° East and carries C- and Ku-band high-throughput spot beams reaching Asia, the Pacific Ocean region, part of North America and Antarctica. That footprint is the reason it matters to a Pacific operator: the mid-Pacific is where commercial geostationary coverage is thinnest, and a spot-beam satellite parked over it is one of the few dense-capacity options between Hawaii and Japan.

HORN-R BULL.purpose: One of a pair of Japanese 6U CubeSats, HORN-L and HORN-R, built by the company BULL to demonstrate a post-mission disposal system. The spacecraft deploys a drag-enhancing device that increases atmospheric resistance so it falls out of orbit faster once its work is done - a passive, propellant-free way for a small satellite to meet debris-mitigation rules, which matters because CubeSats rarely have room for a de-orbit motor.

HORUS.purpose: Two Egyptian imaging satellites placed in orbit by China within three weeks of each other. Neither Cairo nor Beijing published a payload description: Gunter's Space Page lists them as Earth observation satellites launched by China for an undisclosed customer, possibly Egyptian spacecraft jointly built by Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences with the Chinese company DFH. Ownership and capability should therefore be read as assessed rather than documented.

HOTBIRD.purpose: A HOT BIRD satellite: Eutelsat's television broadcast neighbourhood at 13° East, one of the two most-watched orbital positions in Europe and North Africa. Co-locating several high-power Ku-band spacecraft at one longitude means a fixed home dish can receive well over a thousand channels without ever being repointed, which is the whole commercial logic of a broadcast neighbourhood. HOT BIRD 13F and 13G replaced the earlier 13B and 13C spacecraft, which the registry still lists under the EUTE prefix.

HOTSAT-2.purpose: The second satellite of SatVu's high-resolution thermal constellation, built by SSTL for the London company. It uses mid-wave infrared sensors to measure the heat signature of human activity, which is a different question from what optical or radar imagery answers: not what is on the ground but what is running. SatVu markets it for national security, economic intelligence and climate-resilience work, and the ability to distinguish an operating facility from an idle one, day or night, is the reason it is worth a defence analyst's attention.

HYLAS (AVANTI).purpose: Avanti Communications' HYLAS fleet - HYLAS stands for Highly Adaptable Satellite - carries high-throughput Ka-band capacity for the London operator across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. HYLAS-1 was built as an ESA public-private partnership with Avanti to demonstrate a multi-spot-beam Ka- and Ku-band payload that is fully configurable in orbit and to prove the case for low-cost satellite broadband to underserved European markets; Astrium UK led the payload design and ISRO supplied the platform. That in-orbit configurability, together with steerable spot beams, is the fleet's operational point: capacity can be moved to where demand or a contingency appears rather than being fixed when the spacecraft is built.

HYPERFIELD.purpose: A Hyperfield satellite: the first generation of a Finnish commercial hyperspectral constellation flown by Kuva Space. Hyperspectral imaging records dozens to hundreds of narrow contiguous bands rather than three broad ones, which turns an image into a material measurement — crop species and stress, algal blooms in aquaculture waters, and anomalies that a colour camera cannot separate. Kuva pairs the imager with onboard analytics and intends the constellation to grow toward sub-daily revisit.

HYPERION-GR1.organization: Hellenic Ministry of Digital Governance / Open Cosmos Aegean
HYPERION-GR1.purpose: Hyperion GR-1 is the first of seven microsatellites of Greece's national optical imaging constellation, built largely in Athens by Open Cosmos Aegean under the National Microsatellite Programme - the first satellites actually manufactured in Greece rather than bought in. The 100 kg-class spacecraft images panchromatically at 90 cm ground resolution with a 4 m visible/near-infrared multispectral channel, and carries onboard AI processing and inter-satellite links to shorten the time from collection to product. The remaining Hyperion GR satellites are to add submetric optical, hyperspectral, SWIR, IoT and AIS payloads for maritime monitoring.

HYPSO.organization: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)
HYPSO.purpose: A HYPSO satellite: a 6U cubesat from NTNU in Trondheim carrying a hyperspectral imager pointed at the sea. Where an ordinary camera records three broad colour bands, a hyperspectral imager records dozens of narrow ones, and the shape of that spectrum in ocean colour distinguishes phytoplankton species — which is how HYPSO detects and characterises harmful algal blooms along the Norwegian coast, a direct problem for fish farming and for coastal water quality. The mission is also a working demonstration that a university cubesat can produce operational ocean-colour data.

HYSIS.purpose: HysIS, India's hyperspectral imaging satellite, built on the IMS-2 bus to study the Earth's surface in the visible, near infrared and shortwave infrared. A hyperspectral imager splits every pixel into hundreds of narrow bands rather than a handful, which is what allows material identification -- mineralogy, crop stress, water quality, oil on water -- instead of simply mapping shapes.

Hellas Sat 2.purpose: Hellas Sat 2 is the Greek and Cypriot geostationary communications satellite that established the 39 degrees East slot as a direct-to-home broadcasting hotspot for south-eastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean. Hellas Sat is a majority-owned subsidiary of Arabsat, and Hellas Sat 2's capacity was intended to be taken over and expanded by the later Hellas Sat 3 payload flown alongside Inmarsat's EuropaSat.

Hellenic Space Dawn.organization: EMTech Space / Hellenic Ministry of Digital Governance
Hellenic Space Dawn.purpose: Helios and Selene are the two 8U CubeSats of the Hellenic Space Dawn mission, managed by EMTech Space and flown under the Greek national space programme with ESA support - the closing CubeSat mission of the ESA-implemented Greek Connectivity Programme. They pair roughly 16 m Earth observation with onboard edge processing and AAC Clyde Space CubeCAT laser terminals supporting optical inter-satellite and satellite-to-ground links at up to 1 Gbit/s, with the goal of getting imagery to a user within minutes of acquisition. The published application list is led by ship detection and coastal flood monitoring.

HispaSat.purpose: A HispaSat geostationary communications satellite, from the Spanish operator's transatlantic fleet. The 30 degrees West slot carries the bulk of the capacity - 30W-5 and 30W-6 between them provide Ku-, Ka- and C-band coverage spanning Europe, North Africa and the Americas from Canada to Patagonia, optimised over the Iberian peninsula and the Atlantic islands, and their transatlantic reach is what makes HispaSat the default provider for Spanish and Latin American broadcasting and broadband. HispaSat 36W-1, at 36 degrees West, is a different animal: it was the first mission of OHB's SmallGEO platform and carries the RedSAT regenerative processor and a reconfigurable-beam active receive antenna, so its coverage can be re-shaped in orbit.

IHI-SAT2.purpose: IHI-SAT2, a hyperspectral 6U CubeSat for the Japanese heavy-industry group IHI, built by Kongsberg NanoAvionics. Hyperspectral imaging resolves the reflected spectrum finely enough to distinguish vegetation types and condition, and IHI is flying it for forest management and carbon-credit measurement as the first element of a planned Earth-observation constellation.

IMECE.purpose: TUBITAK UZAY's high-resolution optical Earth observation satellite, which the institute describes as Turkiye's first sub-metre resolution imaging spacecraft, flying a submetre panchromatic channel alongside 3.96 m red, green, blue and near-infrared bands. The programme's stated goal was to build the domestic capability to develop imaging-satellite subsystems in-country, and IMECE flew Turkish-developed flight computer, star tracker, X-band antenna and power control hardware. It is the civil-agency counterpart to the GOKTURK reconnaissance line and the technology feeder for later national imaging satellites.

INDEX REIMEI.purpose: REIMEI, JAXA's INnovative-technology Demonstration EXperiment. It was built to show that a small satellite could hold high-accuracy attitude control, and then used that pointing to observe the aurora — imaging the auroral display and simultaneously measuring the electrons falling into it, which is how the fine structure of the aurora is tied to particle precipitation from the magnetosphere.

INMARSAT.purpose: An Inmarsat geostationary satellite. Inmarsat was created in 1979 by the International Maritime Organization to provide satellite safety communications at sea, and it remains the backbone of the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System: Inmarsat C was the first IMO-approved GMDSS service and still carries distress alerting, ship security alerting and maritime safety broadcasts for SOLAS vessels worldwide. The generations divide by band and service — the L-band Inmarsat-3 and Inmarsat-4 spacecraft carry GMDSS and BGAN, and the Inmarsat-5 Global Xpress satellites carry Ka-band broadband, sold at sea as Fleet Xpress and bought in quantity by allied defence users. Any officer who has stood a bridge watch has depended on this constellation whether or not they knew its name.

INMARSAT ALPHASAT.purpose: Alphasat, catalogued as Inmarsat-4A F4, is the fourth Inmarsat-4 spacecraft and the first flight of the European Alphabus platform — at launch in 2013 the largest telecommunications satellite Europe had built. It extends Inmarsat's L-band coverage, including the maritime safety and BGAN services, over Europe, Africa and the Middle East, and it also carries ESA technology-demonstration payloads flown as the price of the agency's share in the development.

INTELSAT.purpose: An Intelsat geostationary communications satellite. Intelsat began in 1964 as the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization, an intergovernmental consortium that owned the world's first commercial international satellite network; it was privatised in 2001 and merged into SES in 2025, and the registry still records the fleet under the old ITSO code. The spacecraft carry C- and Ku-band capacity for broadcasters, telecom carriers, aeronautical and maritime networks, and a substantial share of US and allied government traffic bought commercially. The Epic series — designations ending in E, such as Intelsat 32e and 37e — are the high-throughput spot-beam generation.

INTELSAT GALAXY 28.purpose: Galaxy 28, launched in 2005 as Intelsat Americas 8, is part of the Galaxy series that Hughes Communications began in 1983 and that passed to Intelsat by way of PanAmSat. Galaxy is the American cable-programming neighbourhood: the fleet's C-band capacity is what most US cable and broadcast networks used to reach their affiliates, which is why the C-band spectrum reallocation of the early 2020s was fought over these satellites in particular.

ION SCV-002 Laurentius (PULSE).purpose: D-Orbit's ION SCV-002, named Laurentius, flew the PULSE mission - the flight on which the ION Satellite Carrier stopped being only a precise dispenser and became a transfer vehicle. It deployed twenty satellites, including eight SuperDoves for Planet and twelve SpaceBEEs for Swarm, then fired its Dawn Aerospace thrusters to change its own altitude by up to 10 km and shift its local time of the ascending node, before turning to the in-orbit demonstration of two hosted payloads. That manoeuvring qualified the platform for orbital transportation rather than release-in-place rideshare.

ION SCV-013 Ultimate Hugo (Cosmic Wander.purpose: D-Orbit's thirteenth ION vehicle, named Ultimate Hugo, flew the Cosmic Wander mission - the company's twelfth commercial flight - carrying eighteen spacecraft plus third-party deployers and hosted payloads to a Sun-synchronous orbit for individual release into separate orbital slots. As with every ION, the vehicle itself is the transport and hosting infrastructure: the useful cargo is other operators' satellites and experiments, from startup hardware to university research instruments.

ION SCV-017 Marvelous Mathias (Wish Upon.purpose: D-Orbit's ION SCV Marvelous Mathias flew Wish Upon a Star, the seventeenth commercial mission of the ION Satellite Carrier. Its most notable cargo was the six-CubeSat HERMES Pathfinder gamma-ray burst constellation, which ION released one satellite per day over the week following deployment - a good illustration of why a science constellation buys a tug rather than a plain rideshare, since the spacing between releases sets the geometry the mission needs.

ION Satellite Carrier.purpose: An ION Satellite Carrier: not a free-flying payload but an orbital transfer vehicle - a tug - built and flown by the Italian company D-Orbit. Customers' satellites ride inside a modular 64U dispenser and ION releases them one at a time, changing altitude and local time of the ascending node between deployments so that each spacecraft is dropped into its own slot, or so that a whole constellation batch is phased along a plane in weeks rather than months. Once the deployment phase ends the same vehicle becomes a hosting platform, running third-party payloads and edge-computing experiments for the rest of its life, so an ION in the catalogue is usually carrying other operators' hardware rather than a mission of its own. Each flight is given a mission name and the vehicle a personal name, following naval practice.

IPERDRONE.0.purpose: IPERDRONE.0 is the first flight of an ASI-funded programme, run by CIRA with Tyvak International and Kayser Italia, to build a small reusable re-entry vehicle able to work alongside orbital infrastructure and then bring a payload back to the ground intact. This first mission is a 6U nanosatellite flying the risk-reduction step: autonomous proximity operations around a virtual point, guidance-navigation-and-control validation and optical inspection imagery, with the re-entry and recovery capability deferred to the later IPERDRONE.1 mission.

IPSTAR 1.purpose: Thaicom 4, better known as IPSTAR, the world's first high-throughput satellite, at 119.5 degrees East and now operated by Thailand's National Telecommunications Public Company. Its 87 Ku-band and 10 Ka-band transponders and roughly 45 Gbps of capacity were an order of magnitude beyond conventional fixed-service satellites when it launched in 2005, and it pioneered the two-way multi-spot-beam architecture that every HTS since has used. It remains a significant broadband pool over South and South East Asia and Australia.

IRIDE Eaglet II.organization: Italian Space Agency (ASI) / ESA - IRIDE programme
IRIDE Eaglet II.purpose: An Eaglet II satellite: the second of the six constellations that make up IRIDE, the Italian national Earth-observation system funded through Italy's PNRR recovery plan, procured by ESA and run with ASI. Each Eaglet II is a roughly 25 kg microsatellite built by OHB Italia carrying a multispectral high-resolution optical instrument delivering about 2 m ground resolution, and - unusually for an optical smallsat - an Automatic Identification System receiver, so the same spacecraft that images a coastline can also collect the AIS traffic picture over it. The constellation is sized at 24 satellites and feeds Italy's civil-protection, maritime and coastal monitoring, security and emergency-mapping services.

IRIDE Hawk for Earth Observation.purpose: A Hawk for Earth Observation (HEO) spacecraft: the first of IRIDE's six constellations to fly, built by Argotec on its HAWK microsatellite platform for the Italian government's IRIDE Earth observation programme managed by ESA with ASI. Each satellite is a roughly 70 kg microsatellite carrying a multispectral optical imager working from the visible into the near infrared at about 2.6 m per pixel, with an unusually capable onboard processor - GPU and neural accelerator - so that scenes can be analysed in orbit and only the useful data downlinked. ASI and ESA point the constellation at coastal and marine monitoring, ground motion, hydro-meteorological and climate work, emergencies and security for Italian public authorities.

IRIS-F NCKU.purpose: An IRIS-F nanosatellite — Intelligent Remote-sensing and Internet Satellite — a 3U CubeSat technology demonstrator flown jointly by National Cheng Kung University in Tainan and the Taiwanese company SATORO. The first of the series carried an AIS receiver as an in-orbit verification payload, putting ship-reporting reception on a four-kilogram spacecraft.

IRNSS.purpose: The space segment of NavIC, India's regional satellite navigation system, formerly called the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System. ISRO flies seven satellites -- three geostationary and four in inclined geosynchronous orbits -- and offers a Standard Positioning Service for civil users and a Restricted Service for strategic users, both in L5 and S band. A regional constellation exists because that geometry buys sovereign positioning and timing over the home theatre, out to 1,500 km beyond the Indian boundary, at a fraction of the cost of a global system and without depending on GPS remaining available; the civil signals are designed to interoperate with GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou.

IRNSS R1A.purpose: IRNSS-1A, the first NavIC satellite. All three of its rubidium atomic clocks failed, which took it out of the navigation service and left the constellation running on six satellites until a replacement flew. India's Department of Space has stated that the satellite is still used for messaging services -- disaster alerts and potential fishing zone broadcasts to fishermen -- and that IRNSS-1I was launched in 2018 carrying refurbished clocks to take its place. The same Swiss-built clock type gave comparable trouble on Galileo; the cause was traced to a feed-through capacitor overheating.

ITAMSAT.purpose: ITAMSAT - also designated Italy-OSCAR 26 - is an 11 kg amateur-radio microsatellite built by AMSAT Italia on the AMSAT-NA Microsat bus and launched in 1993 alongside SPOT 3. It carries a Mode JD digital transponder, uplinking on 145 MHz and downlinking on 435 MHz, and runs the PACSAT store-and-forward protocol suite at 1200 bps AX.25: messages are uploaded by one amateur station, held in onboard memory and dumped to another later in the orbit. It is essentially identical to the contemporary PACSAT and LUSAT spacecraft.

ITASAT.purpose: A 6U CubeSat built by Brazil's Instituto Tecnologico de Aeronautica, the air force's engineering institute, originally conceived as an 80 kg microsatellite before being rescoped to CubeSat class to find an affordable launch. It carries a data collection system compatible with Brazil's environmental platform network, a GPS receiver and a camera returning roughly 80 m ground resolution. Its purpose is capability building and student training rather than operational service.

ITUPSAT 1.purpose: A single-unit CubeSat built by the Faculty of Aeronautics and Astronautics at Istanbul Technical University, and the first Turkish university satellite to reach orbit when it launched on PSLV-C14 in September 2009. Its mission goals were to return imagery from a CMOS camera payload and to characterise the behaviour of a passive magnetic stabilisation system, with the wider objective of giving students a hands-on flight project. It is the ancestor of the ITU laboratory that has since built a string of Turkish and partner-nation CubeSats.

JACK-002.purpose: A 3U cubesat filed as carrying a camera for image acquisition of Earth together with an RF link to ground stations. Beyond that the mission is thinly documented: its Korean operator has published no mission page, and the amateur-satellite coordination record is the only public description of what is aboard. Treat the imaging role as stated by the operator to a regulator rather than as a published capability.

JAM-E JAM 1.purpose: Iran's first geostationary communications satellite, owned by Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting and registered internationally as Iran DBS, built in Russia and stationed at 34 degrees East. Its documented function is regulatory as much as operational: it secures and brings into use the ITU frequency filings at that orbital position, which is what a country must do to hold a slot ahead of a larger direct-broadcasting system. No detailed technical specifications have been published.

JAS 2 FUJI.purpose: JAS-2, known on the air as Fuji-OSCAR 29, an amateur radio satellite of the Japan Amateur Radio League. It carries a mode-J linear transponder for voice and CW plus a packet bulletin board, taking uplinks around 145 MHz and returning them near 435 MHz, and also flew a digital voice talker and a space test of new solar cells. Amateur satellites like this one are where a great deal of small-satellite radio practice was first worked out.

JCSAT.purpose: A JCSAT geostationary communications satellite of SKY Perfect JSAT, the leading satellite operator in Asia and a major player in both satellite broadcasting and telecommunications. The JCSAT fleet carries commercial video distribution and regional data traffic over Japan and the wider Asia-Pacific; it is the largest geostationary fleet flown from Japan and the one Japanese broadcasters and enterprises buy capacity on. Individual members differ in band and coverage, and JCSAT 17 and JCSAT 18 are described separately.

JCSAT 17 MOBILE.purpose: JCSAT-17, SKY Perfect JSAT's mobile-communications satellite for Japan and the surrounding region. Lockheed Martin built it as the first Mobile Satellite Service spacecraft on the modernised LM 2100 bus, and it carries a reprogrammable mission processor so the payload can be reshaped in orbit as demand moves rather than being fixed at launch.

JCSAT 18 KACIFIC1.organization: SKY Perfect JSAT / Kacific Broadband Satellites
JCSAT 18 KACIFIC1.purpose: JCSAT-18/Kacific1, a Boeing 702 spacecraft carrying two separate payloads for two operators: SKY Perfect JSAT of Tokyo and Kacific Broadband Satellites of Singapore. The Kacific half sells broadband into the thinly served islands of South East Asia and the Pacific and the far east of Russia, which is also the connectivity backdrop against which disaster response and maritime coordination happen across scattered island states.

JINJUSAT-1B.organization: Jinju City / Korea Testing Laboratory / Gyeongsang National University
JINJUSAT-1B.purpose: A 2U cubesat carrying three cameras, developed by Jinju City with the Korea Testing Laboratory's space components test centre and Gyeongsang National University. It is the first satellite a South Korean local government developed, launched and operated, and the city is candid that growing local space talent matters as much as the Earth photography mission. It replaces JINJUSat-1, which failed to deploy from its rideshare in 2023.

JUGNU.purpose: A 3 kg nanosatellite designed and built by students at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur under ISRO's guidance. Its stated purpose is to prove an indigenously developed camera system imaging the Earth in the near infrared and to test image processing algorithms in orbit; it also flew a GPS receiver and a MEMS inertial unit as technology experiments.

JY1SAT.purpose: Jordan's first satellite: a 1U cubesat from the Masar initiative at the Jordan University of Science and Technology under the Crown Prince Foundation, named for JY1, the amateur radio callsign of the late King Hussein. It carries a 435/145 MHz linear amateur transponder and a slow-scan digital video system that broadcasts stored images and a recorded message, and it is designated Jordan-OSCAR 97.

KANYINI.purpose: Australia's first state-government-funded satellite mission: a 6U CubeSat designed, built and tested entirely in South Australia on Inovor Technologies' Apogee bus, led by SmartSat CRC. It carries a HyperScout 2 hyperspectral and thermal imager with onboard AI processing, and a Myriota Internet-of-Things payload that relays data from ground sensors - the intended users being farmers monitoring water and yields and emergency services tracking bushfire and flood conditions. It demonstrated hyperspectral imaging and the IoT payload on orbit before an anomaly compromised its payload interface computer in 2025.

KENT RIDGE 1.purpose: A National University of Singapore microsatellite built in collaboration with Berlin Space Technologies for hyperspectral imaging applications. It carries three instruments: two medium-resolution hyperspectral payloads using a Fourier transform method and one high-resolution video payload. Hyperspectral data of this kind support water quality, coastal and vegetation discrimination work that broadband multispectral imagers cannot do.

KHALIFASAT.purpose: An Earth observation satellite designed and built at the Space Technology Laboratories of the Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre in Dubai, and considered the first entirely Emirati-made satellite. It followed the two Korean-built DubaiSats and reused the same Satrec SI-300 bus lineage, which is the step that took the UAE from buying spacecraft to building them.

KHAYYAM.purpose: An Iranian high-resolution imaging satellite designed by the Iranian Space Agency but built in Russia by VNIIEM and NPK Barl, under a contract that included technology transfer and Russian assistance with later Iranian-designed satellites in the same family. Neither operator publishes the instrument's performance or its tasking, so what it actually collects is not a matter of public record.

KKS-1 KISEKI.organization: Tokyo Metropolitan College of Industrial Technology
KKS-1 KISEKI.purpose: Kiseki, a 3 kg educational technology satellite built by the Tokyo Metropolitan College of Industrial Technology. Its stated objectives were to demonstrate micro-thrusters, to run basic three-axis attitude control experiments and to take images of land with a small camera — an unusually ambitious combination for a 15 cm cube built by a technical college.

KLEO CONNECT.purpose: A KL-Alpha or KL-Beta test satellite for KLEO Connect, a German company developing a low-Earth-orbit network for the industrial Internet of Things. These four are phase demonstrators rather than service satellites: built by CAS Microspace and carrying Ka-band payloads, they were flown to measure how a Ka-band LEO link behaves in practice, to test suppression of interference into geostationary satellites sharing the band, and to see how commercial-grade electronics survive on orbit. The interference question is the one that matters beyond this company — every non-geostationary Ka constellation has to prove it will not raise the noise floor of the GEO networks already there.

KNACKSAT-2.organization: King Mongkut's University of Technology North Bangkok
KNACKSAT-2.purpose: A 3U multi-payload CubeSat platform developed by the International Institute of Space Technology for Economic Development at King Mongkut's University of Technology North Bangkok, with NBSPACE and Japan's Kyushu Institute of Technology. It is Thailand's first ride-sharing CubeSat: rather than each experimenter building a whole satellite, up to ten user payloads fly in slots on a shared bus and the mission verifies each one in orbit. It was deployed from the International Space Station.

KOMPSAT 2.purpose: The second Arirang satellite and Korea's first one-metre-class imager, developed and flown by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute as the successor to KOMPSAT-1. Its single payload, the Multispectral Camera, worked in one panchromatic band at 1 m ground sample distance and four visible and near-infrared bands at 4 m, over a 15 km swath, feeding mapping, land-resource decisions and large-scale disaster response. KARI retired the mission at the end of 2024.

KOMPSAT 3.purpose: Arirang-3 carries AEISS, a single high-resolution optical imager returning 0.7 m panchromatic and 2.8 m multispectral imagery across a 15 km swath. KARI flies it to meet Korea's own demand for high-resolution imagery, with the stated applications running from cartography and disaster monitoring to environmental, oceanographic and agricultural work. It is well past its design life and still in extended operations.

KOMPSAT 3A.purpose: The first Korean satellite to fly an infrared sensor alongside a sub-metre optical camera. KARI pairs AEISS-A, an electro-optical camera resolving 55 cm, with a mid-wave infrared imager, so one spacecraft maps fine detail by day and reads thermal signatures at night and through weather - forest fires, volcanic activity, urban heat. It was built to serve public safety, disaster and environmental monitoring and resource management.

KOMPSAT 5.purpose: Korea's first radar imaging satellite. Instead of a camera, Arirang-5 carries a synthetic-aperture radar, so it images the peninsula and its approaches through cloud and in darkness - the all-weather, day-night capability that keeps maritime, flood and ice surveillance running when every optical satellite is blind. KARI developed it with Korean industry for public safety, land management and disaster monitoring.

KOMPSAT-7.purpose: The newest Arirang and KARI's successor to KOMPSAT-3A, built to put Korea in the 30 cm-class ultra-high-resolution optical bracket. It carries AEISS-HR, an imager giving about 0.3 m panchromatic and 1.1 to 1.2 m multispectral detail over a 12 km swath, together with an Advanced Infrared Module working in the 3-5 micron mid-wave band for wildfires, volcanic heat and urban heat islands. Arianespace placed it in orbit for KARI to supply Korean government and institutional imagery demand.

KOREASAT 116 (ANASIS-II).purpose: Catalogued as Koreasat 116, but this is not a KT SAT commercial satellite: it is ANASIS-II, the Republic of Korea's first dedicated military spacecraft, a communications satellite for the ROK armed forces. Airbus built it on a Eurostar E3000 bus, delivered as part of the industrial offset for Korea's purchase of 40 F-35 fighters. It gives the ROK Army, Navy and Air Force their own beyond-line-of-sight satellite communications instead of leased commercial or allied capacity; the transponder detail is not published.

KOREASAT 5.organization: KT Corporation / Agency for Defense Development
KOREASAT 5.purpose: South Korea's first combined civil and military communications satellite, flown jointly by KT Corporation and the Agency for Defense Development; the military half is designated ANASIS 1, for Army/Navy/Air Force Satellite Information System. Alongside civil Ku- and C-band capacity it carries SHF transponders reserved for the armed forces, which is where the ROK military first got sovereign satellite communications rather than leased or allied capacity. A solar-array drive failure in 2013 crippled much of its capacity and led to an insurance claim.

KOREASAT 5A.purpose: A KT SAT geostationary comsat launched as the replacement for Koreasat 5's civil capacity, carrying Ku-band transponders plus steerable extended-Ku capacity. Its beams cover Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Indochina and South Asia. KT SAT markets the maritime Ku coverage explicitly, from East Asia to East Africa, which is the capacity behind shipboard VSAT and in-flight connectivity along those routes.

KOREASAT 6 AND 6A.purpose: KT SAT's domestic broadcasting and fixed-service pair at 116 degrees east. Koreasat 6A was ordered from Thales Alenia Space as the direct replacement for Koreasat 6 once that spacecraft reached the end of its operational life, and carries 20 Ku-band transponders for communications plus six more for broadcasting. Between them they feed Skylife satellite television and mobile satellite relay services across South Korea.

KOREASAT 7.purpose: A KT SAT geostationary comsat carrying Ku-band capacity together with a steerable Ka-band payload, covering Korea, the Philippines, Indochina, India and Indonesia. KT SAT sells it for direct-to-home broadcasting, government communications and VSAT networks; the steerable Ka beam can be repointed as demand shifts, which is how a single spacecraft follows a surge rather than waiting for the next one.

KORSAT 425 RADAR SATELLITES.purpose: Despite the similar name these have nothing to do with the KT SAT Koreasat comsats: they are the radar component of Project 425, the Republic of Korea's military reconnaissance constellation, run by the Agency for Defence Development and the Defense Acquisition Program Administration. Korea Aerospace Industries and Hanwha Systems build the spacecraft, with Thales Alenia Space supplying a synthetic-aperture radar whose five-metre antenna unfolds in orbit from 24 petals. Radar is what lets the constellation watch North Korean missile bases, ports and coastline through cloud and at night, complementing the optical member of the same programme.

KORSAT 7 (425 PROJECT EO/IR).purpose: The electro-optical and infrared member of Project 425 and the Republic of Korea's first indigenous military reconnaissance satellite - again unrelated to the KT SAT Koreasat fleet that shares the name. The programme is led by the Agency for Defense Development with KARI, Korea Aerospace Industries and Hanwha Aerospace, and the defence ministry describes an electro-optical infrared telescope in the 30 cm resolution class. Its declared job is near-real-time monitoring of North Korean missile bases and nuclear test facilities, feeding the ROK kill-chain targeting system.

KOYO NCU.purpose: KOYO-1, the Kinetic Optical Yaw Observer, a 3U CubeSat led by National Central University with the Taiwanese startup Aegiverse and the Indian company HEX20. Its purpose was to prove a Taiwan-built fiber-optic gyroscope in orbit — the inertial sensor a satellite or a missile needs to know how it is turning, and a component Taiwan had previously had to import.

KOYOH KANAZAWA.purpose: KOYOH, Kanazawa University's first satellite: a 50 kg-class X-ray transient monitoring and rapid alert spacecraft, selected as a demonstration theme on JAXA's third Innovative Satellite Technology Demonstration flight. It watches for X-ray and gamma-ray transients in order to identify the electromagnetic counterparts of gravitational-wave events and to study how black holes form.

KSLV-II DUMMY.purpose: Not a spacecraft. This is the Nuri test payload, a box-shaped mass simulator of roughly 1,500 kg that KARI released at the end of the third-stage burn so the KSLV-II launcher could be flown against a realistic payload mass. The first one, on Nuri's maiden flight, separated correctly but never reached orbit because the third stage shut down early; this one, on the second flight, did. It carries no instruments and does nothing in orbit but decay.

KSM1.purpose: A Kleos Scouting Mission satellite: four spacecraft flown in a cluster by Kleos Space, a Luxembourg-domiciled company, to geolocate maritime VHF radio transmissions by time and frequency difference of arrival between the members of the formation. The target set is the same one Unseenlabs works — vessels operating without AIS — and the technique is the same in principle, with the difference that Kleos flew multiple receivers in formation rather than characterising signals from a single spacecraft. The company entered administration in 2023; the hardware remains catalogued.

LAOSAT 1.purpose: The first and only Lao communications satellite, contracted in 2010 from China Great Wall Industry Corporation on an in-orbit-delivery basis and operated from 128.5 degrees East by a joint venture between China's APMT and the Lao National Authority for Science and Technology. It carries 14 C-band and 8 Ku-band transponders on a DFH-4S bus for national broadcasting and telecommunications. Like Bolivia's TKSat-1 and Algeria's Alcomsat-1 it is an example of China supplying a small state's entire space communications capability as a single financed package.

LAPAN A3.purpose: LAPAN-A3, also called LAPAN-IPB, a microsatellite built by Indonesia's national aeronautics and space institute with Bogor Agricultural University to monitor food resources and the wider environment across the archipelago. It carries a four-band pushbroom multispectral imager, LISA, at about 18 m ground resolution over a 123 km swath for land use classification, together with an Automatic Identification System receiver that supports maritime awareness by picking up ship AIS broadcasts across a footprint of roughly 2,800 km radius. That AIS payload gives Indonesia its own space-based picture of traffic through its straits.

LAPAN-TUBSAT.purpose: Indonesia's first satellite, later renamed LAPAN-A1, developed jointly by the national institute LAPAN and the Technical University of Berlin under a 2003 agreement, with Indonesian engineers working in Berlin through integration to gain the experience for later indigenous projects. Based on the German DLR-Tubsat design with a new star sensor and structure, it performed Earth observation and attitude control experiments with a steerable video camera. Operations ended in 2013, so it is a defunct object in the catalogue.

LARES.organization: Italian Space Agency (ASI) / Sapienza University of Rome
LARES.purpose: A LAser RElativity Satellite: LARES and LARES 2 are not spacecraft in the usual sense but solid passive spheres covered in corner-cube retroreflectors, with no power, no sensors and no transmitter. Ground stations of the International Laser Ranging Service bounce short laser pulses off them and time the return, so the satellite's orbit can be tracked to a precision that turns it into a test mass. The Italian Space Agency funds the missions with Sapienza University of Rome to measure frame dragging - the Lense-Thirring effect, the dragging of spacetime by Earth's rotation - and the LARES 2 measurement was published in Nature in 2026.

LASARSAT.purpose: LASARsat is the first Czech student-led satellite mission, a 1U CubeSat grown out of a Czech secondary school team's winning entry in the Conrad Challenge and built with Spacemanic, HiLASE, VZLU Aerospace and SkyFox Labs. Its purpose is to test the use of high-power ground lasers for space traffic management and debris mitigation - laser ablation and photon pressure can nudge an uncontrolled object's orbit without touching it - alongside science education and amateur-radio activity.

LATINSAT.purpose: Two of the original 12 kg LatinSat spacecraft, later renamed AprizeSat, built as the start of a store-and-forward low-Earth-orbit constellation for data messaging and fixed and mobile asset tracking. The programme mattered beyond Argentina because later AprizeSat spacecraft added Automatic Identification System receivers and were transferred to exactEarth, becoming part of the first commercial satellite AIS ship-tracking service; several were sold on again to the IoT operator Myriota. These first two are the elderly forerunners of that maritime domain awareness capability rather than contributors to it.

LEAP-1.purpose: Dhruva Space's first commercial mission, flying the company's indigenously developed P-30 platform as a hosted-payload bus. LEAP-1 carries two Australian in-orbit demonstration payloads -- an artificial intelligence processing module from Akula Tech and a hyperspectral imager from Esper Satellites. The LEAP programme sells access to a flight-proven bus so that a customer with an instrument does not have to build a satellite around it.

LEMU-NGE.purpose: A 6U hyperspectral nanosatellite flown by the Chilean company Lemu and the first satellite placed in orbit by a Chilean company. Lemu describes it as the world's first satellite dedicated to biodiversity: its 32-band hyperspectral sensor at better than 5 m ground sample distance is aimed at spectral discrimination of plant species, habitat quality and ecosystem change across native forest, wetland and coastal zones. The name means Forest Eye in Mapudungun.

LEOPARD KYUTECH.organization: Kyushu Institute of Technology / Nanyang Technological University
LEOPARD KYUTECH.purpose: LEOPARD, a 3U CubeSat built by the Kyushu Institute of Technology with Nanyang Technological University and students from seventeen countries, and released into orbit from the Kibo module of the International Space Station. It carries multispectral cameras to monitor horizon glow - the light scattered by the limb of the atmosphere - and demonstrates onboard processing of one-way radio ranging signals.

LIDE.purpose: LIDE is a 12U CubeSat flown by Tyvak International under ESA's ARTES 5G programme to attempt the first live demonstration of direct 5G broadband from a nanosatellite straight to small ground terminals - the very-small-aperture kind carried by civil-protection and search-and-rescue teams - with no dish and no intermediate gateway. It works to the 3GPP Release 17 non-terrestrial-network standard using bent-pipe K/Ka-band transponders supplied by PICOSATS, and is a stepping stone in Europe's road towards 5G and 6G service from low orbit.

LILIUM NCKU.purpose: A Lilium CubeSat built by the CubeSat Research Center at National Cheng Kung University, supported by Taiwan's National Science and Technology Council CubeSat programme, and launched on the same rocket as the first FORMOSAT-8 satellite. The series is part of the university-led half of Taiwan's effort to build a domestic satellite industry rather than buying spacecraft abroad.

LUCAS JDRS-1.purpose: The Japanese Data Relay System spacecraft carrying LUCAS, JAXA's Laser Utilizing Communication System. It sits in geosynchronous orbit and relays data between low-orbit observation satellites and the ground, using an optical link rather than radio to carry far more data and to keep a satellite in contact well beyond the few minutes a ground station pass allows. ALOS-4 was its first user satellite, and the demonstrated user rate of 1.8 Gbit/s is what makes near-real-time delivery of radar imagery practical.

LUMELITE 4.purpose: A 12U Singaporean microsatellite flying an experimental VHF Data Exchange System payload, developed by A*STAR institutes and the National University of Singapore's Satellite Technology and Research Centre with support from the Maritime and Port Authority. VDES is the successor to AIS: it keeps the ship-identification broadcast but adds a two-way data channel, and the Lumelite-4 payload attacks the central problem of space-based reception, which is message collision in dense traffic, using a metamaterial isoflux VHF antenna and a de-collision signal-processing technique. The naval relevance is direct, since better space-based VDES means more reliable vessel tracking and ship-to-shore messaging in exactly the congested waters where AIS reception degrades.

LUNA (ASELSAN).purpose: Nanosatellites in the space-based Internet-of-Things programme of ASELSAN, Turkiye's largest defence electronics company. ASELSAN states that LUNA-1's design, development, production, integration and testing, including its payloads, ground control software and flight computer, were completed by its own engineers, with telemetry received at its Ankara ground station; LUNA-2 followed in March 2026 as the next step in the same programme. The interest for an observer is that a defence prime, not a telecoms startup, is building Turkiye's second sovereign IoT constellation alongside Plan-S's Connecta.

LUR-1.purpose: LUR-1 is the first flight of the LUR microsatellite platform from the Basque company AVS, flown as an end-to-end in-orbit demonstration covering space, ground and user segments. The 57 kg spacecraft carries an Earth-imaging payload at about 1.5 m ground sampling, but the point of the mission is the experiment set flying with it: a MICE mechanical capture interface and nine fiducial markers for proximity operations and end-of-life servicing, a retroreflector, an AVS-built deployable solar array with a shape-memory-alloy release mechanism, and a quantum-key-distribution technology demonstrator with its own single-photon detector.

LUXEOSYS NAOS.assessedBy: the Luxembourg Government's own announcement, which states the programme and its defence ownership but not the sensor's capability
LUXEOSYS NAOS.purpose: NAOS is the satellite of LUXEOSys, the Luxembourg Earth Observation System: a national high-resolution optical imaging capability procured by Luxembourg's Directorate of Defence and launched in August 2025. Luxembourg's stated reason for owning it rather than buying imagery is sovereignty — an intelligence capability under national control that can also be contributed to NATO and EU partners. The detailed performance of the imager is not published.

LYRA (ECHOSTAR GLOBAL).purpose: Lyra is an S-band Internet-of-Things constellation operated by EchoStar Global LLC, an Australian subsidiary of EchoStar, flying under Australia's ITU filings for the SIRION-1 network and built by Astro Digital. The satellites provide global narrowband connectivity for machine-to-machine and other data traffic, and the S-band allocation also serves as EchoStar's platform for continued development of that spectrum portfolio. Deployment is from a rideshare drop-off orbit, with the spacecraft manoeuvring themselves to their operational altitude and expending the remaining propellant to deorbit at end of life.

Lusiada Constellation.purpose: A Lusiada Constellation satellite, built by the Lisbon company LusoSpace and named - like its siblings Camoes, Pessoa, Saramago and Agustina Bessa-Luis - after a Portuguese writer. The four join PoSAT-2 to form a maritime navigation and communications service for the Atlantic, described by its promoters as a 'Waze for the oceans': vessel tracking, safety messaging and data sharing along the transatlantic routes linking Portugal, the Azores and North America. The Portuguese government states the service is for both civilian and military use.

M2 PATHFINDER.organization: UNSW Canberra Space / Royal Australian Air Force
M2 PATHFINDER.purpose: The third UNSW Canberra Space satellite and the second of four flown with the Royal Australian Air Force, built to test an Australian-developed communications architecture and other satellite technologies that would inform the ADF's future space capability. It was designed, assembled and tested in ten months, drawing on lessons from the earlier M1, and served as the risk-reduction flight for the larger M2 mission that followed.

MAGNARO.purpose: MAGNARO - MAGnetically separating NAno-satellite with Rotation for Orbit control - a CubeSat programme of Nagoya University's aerospace vehicle dynamics laboratory. The mission it exists to prove is thruster-less orbit control: the spacecraft spins itself up and then separates into two pieces using electromagnets, converting stored rotation into a change of orbit without propellant. MAGNARO-II is the improved second flight.

MALLIGYONG-1.assessedBy: 38 North (Stimson Center), whose analysis of the launch is the standing open-source assessment; the DPRK has published no imagery and no instrument specification
MALLIGYONG-1.purpose: Malligyong-1 is North Korea's first reconnaissance satellite to reach orbit, launched on 21 November 2023 on a Chollima-1 rocket from the Sohae launching ground after two failed attempts earlier that year. Pyongyang describes it as a military reconnaissance satellite and has published claims about imaging targets in South Korea, Guam and the continental United States; no imagery has been released, and independent analysts assess its optical resolution as modest — useful as a first step and a demonstration of access rather than as a mature ISR capability. What can be verified from outside is the orbit and the fact of the launch, which is why this entry states those and attributes the rest.

MARINA.purpose: MARINA is the fifth Slovak satellite, a 1U CubeSat built by Spacemanic and operated by the Faculty of Aeronautics at the Technical University of Kosice under the privately initiated Satellites with Meaning programme.
