Its scientific payload is an ADVASPACE MiniPix SPACE detector, and the mission exists to measure the space radiation environment - the particle flux that sets the dose budget for hardware and, on crewed or high-inclination missions, for people.

MAROC TUBSAT.purpose: Maroc-TUBSAT, also called Zarkae Al Yamama, is a small Moroccan Earth-observation satellite flown as a cooperation between the Royal Centre for Remote Sensing (CRTS) in Rabat and the TU Berlin aerospace institute, with Morocco responsible for the payload and launch and Berlin for the satellite bus. It follows the TUBSAT line of interactively pointed video imagers, where an operator on the ground steers the spacecraft onto a target during the pass rather than pre-programming the acquisition.

MAUVE.purpose: Mauve is a small ultraviolet-to-visible spectrophotometry satellite, the first science mission of the UK company Blue Skies Space, with the platform supplied and integrated by the Hungarian company C3S and Hungarian astronomers among its users - which is why it is registered to Hungary. Its 13 cm telescope covers roughly 200-700 nm at low spectral resolution and is dedicated to monitoring stellar magnetic activity and flares over long baselines, which bears directly on whether the planets around those stars could be habitable. Blue Skies Space sells access as a subscription science programme rather than through a conventional agency time allocation.

MBZ-SAT.purpose: A 750 kg high-resolution imaging satellite developed by the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre in Dubai, and a substantial step beyond its predecessor KhalifaSat -- roughly double the image capture accuracy, four times the data transfer rate and about ten times the imagery volume. It is used for mapping, environmental monitoring, navigation, infrastructure management and disaster relief across civil and governmental users.

MEASAT.purpose: The operational fleet of MEASAT, Malaysia's satellite operator, providing direct-to-home television, video distribution and data connectivity across Asia-Pacific. MEASAT-3b and the newer MEASAT-3d are co-located at 91.5 degrees East while MEASAT-3a works 160 degrees East covering Asia and Oceania. MEASAT-3d is the most capable of the three, carrying C and Ku-band video payloads, high-throughput Ka-band broadband for Malaysia and the region's first Q/V-band payload, flown to characterise those very high frequencies in the heavy-rain tropical environment where rain fade is the limiting factor.

MENUT.purpose: Menut - Catalan for 'small' - is the second satellite of Catalonia's NewSpace strategy, promoted by the Catalan government and the Institut d'Estudis Espacials de Catalunya and built by Open Cosmos as a 6U CubeSat of under 10 kg. It images at roughly 4.75 m ground sampling over a 19.5 km swath, and the declared purpose is regional: spatial planning and tracking the local effects of the climate crisis rather than a commercial imaging service.

MEXSAT.purpose: Two elements of MEXSAT, the turnkey satellite communications system Mexico bought from Boeing for its Ministry of Communications and Transportation, delivered with two ground sites at Hermosillo and government user terminals. Boeing states the system provides secure communications for Mexico's national security needs as well as civil telecommunications coverage. MEXSAT 3, also called Bicentenario, is the extended C and Ku-band fixed-service satellite for rural broadband; Morelos 3 is a 702HP geomobile spacecraft with a 22 m L-band reflector, giving handheld and vehicle-mounted mobile satellite service to Mexican government and emergency users.

MICE-1.purpose: MICE-1 - Maritime Identification and Communication System 1 - is a CubeSat designed and built in Alexandroupolis by Prisma Electronics under Greece's national space programme, and the first Greek nanosatellite dedicated to maritime IoT. It carries two payloads that matter directly to a maritime picture: a space-based AIS receiver for ship tracking beyond coastal VHF range, and an S-band IoT transceiver feeding Prisma's LAROS system, which collects and encrypts sensor data from vessels and remote infrastructure outside terrestrial coverage. It was the first mission of the Hellenic CubeSat programme to complete all its technical and operational objectives.

MIKROGLOB-1.purpose: MikroGLOB-1, named PIRX-1 after Stanislaw Lem's Pilot Pirx, is the first Polish optical reconnaissance satellite of the military MikroGLOB programme - the first of four contracted in December 2024 between Poland's Armament Agency and Creotech Instruments, built on the company's HyperSat platform. The declared purpose is to widen the Polish armed forces' own satellite reconnaissance capability, imaging in the visible bands (panchromatic, red, green, blue) and in the near infrared, with the whole set to reach low orbit by 2027. It is the optical half of a pair: the parallel POLSARIS programme supplies the radar constellation. The instrument's resolution is not published.

MILSPACE2.organization: Norwegian and Netherlands Ministries of Defence (MilSpace2)
MILSPACE2.purpose: Birkeland and Huygens are the two nanosatellites of MilSpace2, a joint programme of the Norwegian and Netherlands Ministries of Defence with FFI, TNO, NLR and NanoAvionics. They fly as a pair, close together, and geolocate radar and other radio emitters by comparing the time and frequency at which each spacecraft receives the same signal — a technique that needs two or more receivers with a known separation, which is why they were launched and are operated together. The programme's point is to show that a militarily useful electronic-intelligence capability can be built from nanosatellites rather than from a national-technical-means budget.

MIMAN.purpose: A 3U cubesat from Yonsei University, one of the four student payloads deployed on Nuri's second flight; its name stands for Monochrome Imaging for Monitoring Aerosol by Nanosatellite. It images fine dust over the Korean peninsula at higher spatial resolution than the geostationary GEO-KOMPSAT-2B can reach, the trade being that a low-orbit satellite sees a given area far less often. The corrected imagery goes to the fine-dust research team as research data and as auxiliary data for cloud masking.

MIMIR.purpose: Mimir-1 is Space Norway's in-orbit laboratory: a satellite sold as test capacity rather than as a mission, on which customers fly and operate their own Earth-observation, communications and navigation experiments without procuring a spacecraft. It launched alongside AISSat-4 in March 2026 and is operated by Space Norway from Norway.

MISRSAT-2.purpose: An Egyptian remote sensing satellite built as a joint Egyptian Space Agency and Chinese project, carrying a high-resolution imager at 2 m panchromatic and 8 m colour. Its significance to Egypt is industrial as much as operational: China supplied bus units and the flight model was assembled, integrated and tested at the Egyptian Space Agency's own facility outside Cairo before being returned to China for launch.

MOHAMMED VI.assessedBy: Gunter's Space Page, which records the procurement as a high-resolution optical reconnaissance system; Morocco has not published the sensor's performance
MOHAMMED VI.purpose: A Mohammed VI satellite: Morocco's first optical imaging spacecraft, a pair built by Airbus Defence and Space and Thales Alenia Space on the AstroSat-1000 bus and operated by the Moroccan Ministry of Defence. The published mission list is dual-use — mapping and land survey, regional development, agricultural monitoring, disaster prevention and management, environmental change and desertification — and includes border and coastal surveillance, which is the reconnaissance half stated in as many words. The imaging performance is not published.

MOST (HUMBLE SPACE TELESCOPE).purpose: Microvariability and Oscillations of Stars, Canada's first space telescope and for years the smallest one in orbit, which earned it the nickname the Humble Space Telescope. It performs ultra-high-precision photometry, measuring the tiny brightness oscillations that reveal a star's internal structure and age, and it was the first spacecraft dedicated to asteroseismology - the technique later scaled up by CoRoT and Kepler. Its precision pointing, built on Canadian reaction-wheel work, was the heritage that made NEOSSat possible.

NANOSAT C BR1.organization: INPE / Federal University of Santa Maria
NANOSAT C BR1.purpose: Brazil's first CubeSat, developed by INPE's Southern Regional Space Research Centre with the Federal University of Santa Maria. Its science mission is to measure the geomagnetic field over the South Atlantic Magnetic Anomaly and the Brazilian sector of the equatorial ionospheric electrojet using a three-axis magnetometer, and its technology mission is to flight-test Brazilian-designed integrated circuits for radiation tolerance. The anomaly is the region where trapped-particle flux dips closest to Earth, so it drives single-event upsets and HF propagation disturbances that matter to anyone operating electronics or radios in the South Atlantic.

NAPA-1.purpose: The first satellite of the Royal Thai Air Force and the first Earth observation CubeSat operated by the Thai government, a 6U spacecraft built by the Dutch company ISISPACE. It carries a Gecko imager from SCS Space and a prototype Simera Sense TriScape100, and the declared mission is disaster monitoring and response: floods, wildfires, earthquakes, landslides and air quality. It was a deliberately cheap entry point, reported at under 100 million baht, into military space operations.

NEE (ECUADOR).purpose: The two spacecraft of Ecuador's NEE programme, built by the Ecuadorian Civilian Space Agency as 1U CubeSats with deployable solar wings. NEE-01 Pegaso, launched in April 2013, was Ecuador's first satellite and carried a combined visible and infrared camera able to transmit live video from orbit; NEE-02 Krysaor followed in November 2013. Pegaso's attitude control and antennas were probably damaged by a close approach with a catalogued object about a month after launch, which makes the pair an early and often-cited case study in conjunction risk for cubesats.

NEMO-HD.organization: SPACE-SI (Slovenian Centre of Excellence for Space Sciences and Technologies)
NEMO-HD.purpose: NEMO-HD - Next-generation Earth Monitoring and Observation, High Definition - is Slovenia's first microsatellite, developed by the SPACE-SI centre of excellence with the University of Toronto's Space Flight Laboratory. Its distinguishing feature is real-time video: alongside four-band multispectral stills at about 2.8 m pan-sharpened resolution over a 10 km swath, both its primary and secondary instruments capture high-definition video at 25 frames per second, H.264 encoded and downlinked live - an interactive, operator-in-the-loop mode rather than the usual store-and-forward imaging.

NEONSAT.purpose: The New-space Earth Observation Satellite constellation for national safety: eleven microsatellites developed by the Satellite Technology Research Center at KAIST, each carrying a camera system resolving about one metre. It is Korea's first mass-produced satellite system, built to give near-real-time revisit over the Korean peninsula for natural disasters and, the government states plainly, for national-security use. NEONSAT-1 opened the series and NEONSAT-1A followed to test improvements before the remaining spacecraft fly.

NEOSSAT.organization: Canadian Space Agency / Defence Research and Development Canada
NEOSSAT.purpose: A suitcase-sized Canadian space telescope with a deliberately dual mission: space astronomy and orbital space surveillance. Built by CSA with Defence Research and Development Canada, it was the world's first space telescope dedicated to detecting and tracking asteroids, comets, satellites and space debris, and its extended baffle lets it observe at low solar elongation, close to the Sun, where ground telescopes cannot look. The space-domain-awareness half of the job is the part an operator should note: a 15 cm agile telescope in polar orbit tracking other people's spacecraft is a small but real national SSA sensor.

NESS.purpose: NESS is a small satellite developed by the Toulouse manufacturer U-Space with CNES to detect terrestrial sources of radio interference. Interference into satellite uplinks — accidental or deliberate — is normally hunted from the ground by triangulating between gateways, which works badly over the ocean and not at all where there are no gateways; a spacecraft that can localise the emitter directly is the alternative.

NETSAT.organization: University of Würzburg / Zentrum für Telematik
NETSAT.purpose: A NetSat spacecraft: four identical 3U cubesats flown by the Zentrum für Telematik in Würzburg to demonstrate autonomous formation control in three dimensions — the satellites organise their own relative geometry rather than being commanded into it from the ground. The reason to want that is sensing: several spacecraft holding a known three-dimensional arrangement can image a target from multiple angles at once, which is what makes tomographic and true three-dimensional observation from orbit possible.

NEXSAT-1.purpose: An experimental Egyptian remote sensing microsatellite developed with Germany's Berlin Space Technologies, with Egyptian Space Agency engineers taking on the critical operating software and systems. EgSA presents it as a localisation step -- proving Egyptian design and software capability for microsatellites ahead of domestic manufacturing -- rather than as an operational imaging asset.

NEXTSAT-1.purpose: The first of KAIST's next-generation small satellites, built at its Satellite Technology Research Center to prove a standardised 100 kg platform and fly real science on it at the same time. It carries the Instrument for the Study of Space Storms, which measures plasma density and energetic particle flux in near-Earth space, and NISS, a near-infrared imaging spectrometer from the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute used for star-formation history. Seven Korean-developed core space technologies were qualified in orbit alongside them, the point being import substitution.

NEXTSAT-2.purpose: The second of KAIST's next-generation small satellites, designed and developed at its Satellite Technology Research Center as an X-band synthetic-aperture radar technology demonstration, and flown as the payload of the third flight of Korea's Nuri launcher. Fitting a working radar imager into a 150 kg-class satellite is the step that makes an affordable all-weather smallsat constellation possible, which is why the demonstration mattered more than the imagery it returned.

NIGCOMSAT 1R.purpose: The Nigerian Communications Satellite, operated by the government-owned company NIGCOMSAT Ltd and delivered in orbit by China Great Wall Industry Corporation on a DFH-4 bus as the free replacement for NigComSat-1, which failed in 2008 after a solar array anomaly. NIGCOMSAT describes it as a quad-band satellite carrying C, Ku, Ka and L-band payloads from 42.5 degrees East, covering West, Central and South East Africa plus parts of Europe and Asia. The L-band payload is the unusual element for an African comsat and was intended to support navigation augmentation and mobile services.

NIGERIASAT.purpose: Two SSTL-built Earth observation satellites launched together in August 2011 for Nigeria's National Space Research and Development Agency and contributed to the Disaster Monitoring Constellation. NigeriaSat-2 is the high-resolution element on the agile SSTL-300 bus, delivering 2.5 m panchromatic and 5 m multispectral imagery across a 20 km swath; NigeriaSat-X is a 22 m wide-swath spacecraft that doubled as the training model built in Guildford by a team of Nigerian engineers who then commissioned it in orbit. Their declared uses are crop monitoring and food security, urban planning and disaster relief across Africa.

NIGHTJAR RAPIDTEK.purpose: Nightjar, a 3U CubeSat technology demonstrator developed by Rapidtek in cooperation with the Taiwan Space Agency. It carries a Ku-band software-defined radio payload to prove high-speed space-to-ground Internet-of-Things communications, and was Rapidtek's first in-orbit demonstration of a complete communications satellite system before the larger Black Kite spacecraft followed.

NILESAT.purpose: The Egyptian Satellite Company's direct-to-home broadcasting fleet at 7 degrees West, the principal television hot spot for the Middle East and North Africa. Nilesat 301 carries 32 Ku-band transponders plus six Ka-band transponders for broadband over Egypt, and extends DTH coverage from MENA into the southern part of Africa and the Nile Basin. The operator also advertises anti-jamming channels and geolocation of jammers, which is a standing operational problem for broadcast satellites over this region.

NIMIQ (TELESAT DTH).purpose: Telesat's Nimiq series, the direct-broadcast half of the Canadian fleet. Telesat states that Nimiq 2, 4, 5 and 6 give broadcasters and programmers the capability to deliver video content to homes and cable headends; the customers are Bell Satellite TV in Canada and EchoStar's Dish Network in the United States, with Nimiq 5's entire available payload committed to EchoStar. The name was chosen in a 1998 public naming contest and is an Inuit word for a thing that binds others together.

NISAR.purpose: The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar mission, and the first radar satellite to carry two SAR frequencies on one spacecraft: NASA's L-band at 24 cm wavelength and ISRO's S-band at 9.4 cm. The two wavelengths interact differently with vegetation, soil and ice, so the pair separates canopy from ground and surface from volume scattering in a way no single-frequency radar can. Its declared objective is to measure and understand changes in Earth's land, ice, water and vegetation -- ground deformation from earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides and subsidence at centimetre scale -- and the data are released openly, L-band through the Alaska Satellite Facility and S-band through ISRO's Bhoonidhi portal.

NORSAT.purpose: A NorSat microsatellite: Norway flies these to watch shipping across more than two million square kilometres of sea area it is responsible for. Every one of them carries an AIS receiver, so the constellation picks up the self-reported position of cooperating vessels far beyond coastal VHF range. NorSat-3 added an experimental navigation radar detector for the vessels that do not cooperate — a ship can silence its AIS but it will generally keep its radar running — and that instrument is a joint effort of the Norwegian Coastal Administration, the Norwegian Space Agency and the Norwegian Armed Forces. NorSat-1 and 2 also carry space-weather and communications payloads. Small, cheap and specific: this is what a maritime nation buys when it needs coverage rather than resolution.

NORWAY AISSAT 4.purpose: AISSat-4 continues Norway's original line of dedicated ship-tracking nanosatellites, which began with AISSat-1 in 2010 and proved that a satellite the size of a shoebox could receive AIS transmissions from orbit and give a coastal state a picture of traffic hundreds of miles offshore. The problem that makes it hard is collisions: AIS was designed for ship-to-ship use over the horizon, so from orbit a single receiver hears thousands of overlapping transmissions in dense sea areas, and most of the engineering effort goes into pulling the messages apart.

NOVASAR 1.purpose: A small S-band synthetic aperture radar satellite built and operated by SSTL, part-funded by the UK government, with the SAR payload developed by Airbus in Portsmouth. It carries a dedicated maritime surveillance mode and an Automatic Identification System receiver, so a single pass yields both radar ship detections and the cooperative AIS picture to correlate them against - the direct route to identifying the contact that does not report. Dstl has published work using NovaSAR imagery for automated ship detection in support of maritime domain awareness, and capacity shares are held by the UK Space Agency, CSIRO in Australia, ISRO and the Philippines' DOST-ASTI.

NSS.purpose: A geostationary satellite of the former New Skies Satellites fleet, now operated by SES. New Skies was spun out of Intelsat in 1998 to run part of the intergovernmental organisation's commercial capacity and was acquired by SES in 2006; the NSS spacecraft kept their names and carry wide-beam C- and Ku-band capacity over the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Ocean regions. Wide-beam C-band of this kind is what long-haul shipping, oil and gas, and government users still buy when a spot-beam network does not reach.

NULINK.purpose: The first two satellites of the Internet-of-Things communications constellation being built by the Singapore company NuSpace, flown as 3 kg 3U CubeSats with miniature Hall-effect thrusters for orbit maintenance. NuSpace sells sensor-to-satellite connectivity across South East Asia, which is the market gap left by patchy terrestrial coverage across the archipelagic states.

NUSANTARA SATU.purpose: Also known as PSN-6, a Space Systems/Loral geostationary satellite ordered by PT Pasifik Satelit Nusantara, Indonesia's first private satellite operator. It carries conventional wide-beam capacity for South East Asia plus a high-throughput payload dedicated to Indonesia, and it shared its Falcon 9 with the Beresheet lunar lander. PSN's business is connecting the archipelago's dispersed islands where fibre does not reach.

NUSANTARA TIGA.purpose: Also called SATRIA-1, Indonesia's first very-high-throughput satellite, built by Thales Alenia Space on a fully electric Spacebus Neo platform for the Satelit Nusantara Tiga consortium on behalf of the Indonesian Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. It offers 150 Gbps spread across more than a hundred beams and exists to bridge the digital divide: its capacity is committed to schools, hospitals, public buildings and regional government facilities on islands that no terrestrial or existing satellite system reaches. It is a universal-service asset rather than a commercial broadcast satellite.

NUVIEW ALPHA / BRAVO (ANUVU).purpose: Two Astranis MicroGEO satellites leased to Anuvu, which uses them for in-flight and maritime connectivity - internet aboard aircraft and cruise ships. Small dedicated geostationary spacecraft suit that mobility market well because capacity can be committed to specific ocean and air routes rather than shared across a continental beam. Note that despite the name these are communications satellites; they are unrelated to the separate US company NUVIEW that is developing spaceborne lidar.

NVS-01.purpose: The first of NavIC's second-generation NVS satellites, the series intended to sustain and augment the constellation with enhanced features. NVS-01 adds a civil L1-band signal to the existing L5 and S-band services -- L1 is the band ordinary GPS receivers already use, so it is the change that makes NavIC practical in mass-market and handheld equipment -- and it was the first NavIC satellite to fly an indigenous Indian atomic clock, after imported rubidium clocks failed on the first-generation spacecraft.

NanoSat (INTA).purpose: A NanoSat microsatellite of INTA, Spain's national aerospace technology institute. Beyond qualifying INTA-designed attitude sensors and subsystems, the operational job of these 20-odd kilogram spacecraft is store-and-forward communications: they collect traffic on a polar orbit and dump it when they pass over the control centre at Torrejon or over deployable nano-terminals. INTA states the main mission as linking remote sites - the Spanish Antarctic base and the Navy-crewed research vessel Hesperides - back to Spain, which is the classic naval use of a small store-and- forward satellite: a low-rate but sovereign link to a unit far outside terrestrial coverage.

O3B.purpose: An O3b satellite: SES's medium-Earth-orbit constellation, flying in a near-equatorial ring about 8,000 km up. The name is short for "the Other 3 Billion", the people who had no broadband when the system was conceived. The point of MEO is latency — a round trip through 8,000 km is roughly a fifth of the delay through a geostationary satellite at 36,000 km — which makes it usable for interactive traffic that GEO handles badly, and O3b is heavily used by cruise ships, island states and remote government sites. The equatorial ring is also its limit: coverage falls away at high latitudes, which is why polar users cannot rely on it.

O3B MPOWER.purpose: An O3b mPOWER satellite: SES's second-generation medium-Earth-orbit system, again at about 8,000 km, built by Boeing and in global service since April 2024. Each spacecraft is software-defined and steers thousands of beams, so capacity can be moved to where the demand is rather than being fixed at build time — a carrier group, a disaster response or a cruise route can be given bandwidth on the day. The registry spells these four different ways, including O3BF03 and SES MPOWER-A F2, which is why they are keyed here by catalog number rather than by name.

OBSERVER-1A.purpose: Nara Space's first standard nanosatellite: a 16U cubesat platform carrying an optical camera at about 1.5 m ground sample distance, with an X-band imagery downlink. It is the company's heritage demonstrator rather than an operational imaging service - the same Observer bus, rated to carry up to 12 kg of payload, is what Nara Space then sold into later missions including the Gyeonggi climate satellite.

OCEANSAT 2.purpose: An ocean-observation satellite carrying three payloads: an Ocean Colour Monitor, a Ku-band pencil-beam scatterometer built by ISRO, and the Italian Space Agency's ROSA radio-occultation sounder. The scatterometer is the METOC instrument -- it derives ocean surface wind speed and direction from radar backscatter off wind-driven capillary waves, feeding cyclone tracking and marine forecasting over the Indian Ocean. Ocean colour gives chlorophyll and turbidity; radio occultation returns atmospheric temperature and humidity profiles for numerical weather prediction.

OMNI-M1.purpose: Catalogued as OMNI-M1, this spacecraft is ICO F-2, the foundation satellite of the ICO Global Communications medium-earth-orbit mobile telephony system. It was released directly into a circular medium Earth orbit at about 5,460 nautical miles rather than into a transfer orbit. A MEO constellation of this kind was meant to give handheld terminals shorter path delay and higher elevation angles than a geostationary mobile satellite; the full constellation was never built out.

OPTISAT.purpose: OptiSat is a 6U CubeSat designed, built and operated by Planetek Hellas under contract to ESA within the Greek National Microsatellite Programme. Its purpose is to demonstrate secure optical - laser - satellite communications combined with onboard processing of Earth-observation data, so that imagery is reduced in orbit and then downlinked over a high-rate optical link rather than a congested radio one. It flew as part of a wider Greek laser-terminal test campaign alongside PeakSat and ERMIS-3.

OPTOS.purpose: OPTOS is a low-cost triple-cube nanosatellite built in-house by INTA to prove out a set of spacecraft-engineering ideas rather than to return data about the Earth. Its distinguishing feature is an optical wireless internal data bus: the on-board data handling is distributed across FPGAs and programmable logic devices that talk to each other over free-space optical links running a reduced CAN protocol, removing much of the internal harness, and the structure is built from composite materials.

OPTUS (D1 / D3 / 10).purpose: Optus is Australia's most experienced satellite owner-operator, and this Ku-band geostationary fleet carries television, voice and data across Australia, New Zealand and as far south as McMurdo Sound in Antarctica, controlled from an operations centre at Belrose in New South Wales with stations in Western Australia, the ACT and South Australia. Optus D3 carries both fixed-satellite-service and broadcast-satellite-service Ku payloads, including FSS transponders dedicated to New Zealand. The Antarctic reach is the operationally distinctive part: very few commercial fleets advertise coverage that far south.

OQ TECHNOLOGY MACSAT.purpose: MACSAT is a pathfinder for satellite 5G: OQ Technology, funded by the Luxembourg government through ESA, flies it to demonstrate narrowband Internet-of-Things service to ordinary cellular devices using frequencies shared with terrestrial mobile networks. The significance is the standard rather than the spacecraft — if a satellite can serve an unmodified 5G IoT device, the terminal problem that has always limited satellite machine-to-machine service largely disappears.

ORBASTRO.purpose: Spacecraft flown by OrbAstro, a UK smallsat manufacturer that builds and operates missions for customers on its own platforms rather than selling buses alone. JEN-1, the twelfth OrbAstro satellite launched, is a 100 kg-class constellation-grade spacecraft configured, built, qualified, delivered and launched within five months of project start for an undisclosed commercial customer, flown to demonstrate rapid constellation deployment and streamlined operations. Payload details for these missions have not been published.

OROratech FOREST.purpose: A FOREST satellite: OroraTech of Munich flies these 8U cubesats carrying mid- and long-wave thermal infrared imagers to detect wildfires and measure land surface temperature. Thermal infrared is the band in which a fire is unmistakable and in which nothing else on the ground looks like one, and the commercial argument is revisit — a fire that is found in twenty minutes is a different problem from one found in four hours. Forest-16, 17, 18 and 19 were launched in May 2026 as the Hellenic Fire System, making Greece the first country to field a sovereign operational constellation dedicated to wildfire detection.

OSCAR 10.purpose: AMSAT-OSCAR 10, built by AMSAT-DL and launched in 1983 as Phase 3-B, was the first amateur-radio satellite in a high Molniya-type orbit — roughly 4,000 km at perigee and 35,000 km at apogee — and it changed what amateur satellite operation meant. From low orbit a pass lasts about ten minutes; from this orbit a single access window lasted hours and spanned continents, which put intercontinental contacts within reach of modest stations. Radiation damage to its computer eventually left it usable only intermittently, and it is now an uncontrolled but still-transmitting relic.

OSCAR 19 (LUSAT).purpose: LUSAT-1, also known as OSCAR-19, was Argentina's first satellite, launched in January 1990 and built by AMSAT Argentina on an AMSAT-NA microsatellite bus. It carried a store-and-forward amateur radio digital message system with a 145 MHz uplink and 437 MHz downlinks plus a CCD camera. Its digital service has long since ended, but the 437.125 MHz CW beacon has continued to be heard, making it one of the longest-lived amateur spacecraft in orbit.

OVZON 3.purpose: Ovzon 3 is a small geostationary communications satellite built around two features that matter to a mobile user: high-power steerable spot beams that can be moved to a new area within minutes, and an onboard processor that lets the satellite route traffic without a fixed ground hub. The Swedish operator sells it as SATCOM-as-a-service for users who need a lot of throughput from a very small, transportable terminal, and the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration is among its customers.

Open Cosmos MR (Ka-band).purpose: MR-1 and MR-2 are the first two spacecraft of Open Cosmos's own Ka-band low-orbit communications constellation, extending the company beyond the Earth-observation smallsats it has built for Spanish, Portuguese and Greek customers into dedicated high-capacity links. They were designed and integrated on the company's modular smallsat platform with engineering teams across Spain, Portugal and Greece, and operate on high-priority Ka-band spectrum granted through Liechtenstein, the basis of the company's bid for a sovereign European LEO broadband capability.

PADRE.organization: UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory / NASA
PADRE.purpose: PADRE - the solar PolArization and Directivity X-Ray Experiment - is a NASA CubeSat led by the Space Sciences Laboratory at UC Berkeley, flown on an EnduroSat platform, which is why it is catalogued under Bulgaria. It is a 12U spinner that measures the polarisation and directivity of the hard X-rays emitted during solar flares, in order to settle whether the accelerated electrons travel as a collimated beam or spread out as a quasi-isotropic cloud - a direct constraint on how flares convert magnetic energy into particle acceleration, and therefore on the physics behind space-weather events.

PAKSAT 1R.purpose: Pakistan's Chinese-built geostationary communications satellite at 38 degrees East, operated by SUPARCO and marketed as commercial leased capacity and managed services. It carries C and Ku-band payloads: high-power Ku over Pakistan and the rest of South and Central Asia for small-antenna users, and a C-band beam used for cellular backhaul and IP trunking across South Asia, the Middle East, Africa and parts of Central Asia.

PAKSAT MM1R.purpose: PakSat-MM1, a Chinese-built high-power multi-mission satellite at 38.2 degrees East. Besides C, Ku and Ka-band communications for broadband, television, mobile backhaul and VSAT connectivity, it carries an L-band satellite-based augmentation payload -- a GNSS correction and integrity broadcast of the same class as India's GAGAN or the American WAAS, which is the piece of infrastructure a country needs before GNSS can be used for precision approach and other safety-of-life work.

PAKTES 1A.purpose: Pakistan Technology Evaluation Satellite-1A, a 285 kg spacecraft carrying an optical payload and, unlike its co-passenger PRSS-1, designed and developed indigenously by SUPARCO's own engineers with a three-year design life. It is a national capability demonstrator: the point was to prove that Pakistan could build the satellite, not merely operate one.

PANDORE.purpose: Pandore is an in-orbit demonstration flown by the Toulouse manufacturer U-Space, carrying Safran's Synchrocube payload: it broadcasts timing signals from low Earth orbit to test LEO-based positioning and time synchronisation. That is the same argument Europe is making with the Celeste programme — a signal from 500 km is far stronger and its geometry changes far faster than one from GNSS altitude, which makes it harder to jam and quicker to converge — being tested here commercially. It flew on Transporter-13 alongside its sister satellite SOAP, both the first from U-Space's new Toulouse factory.

PAUSAT-1.organization: Air University Pakistan / Istanbul Technical University
PAUSAT-1.purpose: A 16U CubeSat carrying a high-resolution multispectral imager, designed and built by Istanbul Technical University's Space Systems Design and Test Laboratory in collaboration with Air University Pakistan, which owns and operates it. ITU records it as the eighth satellite produced by that laboratory. Despite its Turkish catalogue registration it is a Pakistani university imaging mission, which is worth noting before it is read as a Turkish national asset.

PERUSAT 1.purpose: PerúSAT-1 is Peru's first Earth-observation satellite, ordered by the Peruvian government for its space agency CONIDA and built by Airbus in under two years on the AstroBus-300 platform. It carries a NAOMI silicon-carbide optical instrument returning 0.7 m panchromatic and 2 m multispectral imagery, and it is operated from a national ground segment for mapping, resource management, disaster response and border and coastal surveillance.

PETREL LCTF.purpose: PETREL, the Platform for Extra and Terrestrial Remote Examination with LCTF, built by the Tokyo Institute of Technology and flown on JAXA's Innovative Satellite Technology Demonstration programme. Its liquid-crystal tunable-filter multispectral camera does two jobs: an ultraviolet sky survey for time-domain astronomy, and spectroscopic observation of the Earth. It is a pathfinder for the ULTRASAT mission.

PHISAT 2.purpose: ESA's Phi-sat-2, a 6U CubeSat built by Open Cosmos to demonstrate running artificial intelligence on the spacecraft rather than on the ground. Its multispectral imager feeds an onboard AI computer running uploadable apps: cloud detection offered as a service to other apps, deep image compression, a street-map generator for disaster response, and - the one with operational meaning here - autonomous detection and classification of marine vessels for maritime security. New apps can be uploaded after launch, which is the architectural point of the mission.

PIAST.organization: Polish Ministry of National Defence / Military University of Technology (WAT)
PIAST.purpose: A PIAST spacecraft - Polish ImAging SaTellites - a constellation of optoelectronic imaging nanosatellites built for the Polish armed forces under the Ministry of National Defence's SZAFIR programme, led by the Military University of Technology with Creotech Instruments, Scanway, PCO, the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and the Lukasiewicz Institute of Aviation. The point of the project is sovereign capability rather than resolution records: a Polish optical instrument on a Polish platform, tasked and controlled from a mission control centre in Poland, with the imagery processed on Polish ground software. The operators describe it as dual-use and publish sample imagery of targets worldwide.

PISAT.purpose: A nanosatellite developed by PES University, Bangalore and its consortium under ISRO's technical guidance, carrying a GomSpace NanoCam imaging payload for Earth remote sensing at roughly 91 m per pixel. Its declared objectives are as much about the ground segment as the spacecraft -- tracking, maintaining and operating the satellite is itself part of the mission, which is what a university programme is really buying.

PLATERO.purpose: Platero is a 6U CubeSat commissioned by the Andalusian regional government through its agriculture and fisheries agency AGAPA and built by Open Cosmos. It combines a multispectral camera with an IoT radio that talks directly to ground sensors, and a Ubotica CogniSAT AI board that fuses the two on board in real time, so soil-moisture, water-quality, wildlife and crop-stress indicators are produced in orbit rather than assembled later on the ground. The regional purpose is monitoring biodiversity, desertification, wildfires and floods to inform Andalusian environmental policy.

PLEIADES.purpose: A Pléiades very-high-resolution optical imaging satellite. CNES built the pair — Pléiades 1A and 1B — as an explicitly dual-use system: 70 cm colour imagery resampled to 50 cm, of any point on the globe within 24 hours, for civil and military users alike, with French defence holding priority tasking. The two spacecraft are phased 180° apart in the same orbit as SPOT 6 and 7, so the four together give a daily revisit at high resolution. Airbus markets the civil capacity commercially, which is why the same satellite appears in a national programme and in a commercial imagery catalogue.

PNEO.purpose: A Pléiades Neo satellite: Airbus's fully self-funded successor to the CNES Pléiades pair, imaging at 30 cm native resolution. The design point is reactivity rather than resolution alone — the constellation is built to be retasked and to deliver within hours, which is what matters when the question is what changed at a port or an airfield since yesterday rather than what a place looks like in general.

POEM.purpose: Not satellites in the ordinary sense: POEM is the spent fourth stage of a PSLV, kept alive after it has injected its primary payloads and operated as an orbital platform. ISRO describes it as giving the scientific community an opportunity to run in-orbit microgravity experiments for up to three months on hardware that would otherwise become debris the moment the launch was over. The platform has grown with each flight -- POEM-4 hosted 24 payloads from ISRO centres, universities and start-ups.

POLYITAN 1.purpose: Ukraine's first nanosatellite, a 1U CubeSat built by students and staff at the Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute with the Ukrainian amateur radio community. Its objectives were to establish a national small-satellite platform and ground segment from scratch and to fly a Sun sensor, an attitude determination and control system, and a GLONASS/GPS navigation subsystem. Designed for perhaps a year or two of life, it was still operating a decade after launch, which the university submitted to the Ukrainian Book of Records.

POSAT 2.purpose: PoSAT-2, named for Portugal's first satellite, is LusoSpace's first spacecraft and the start of a planned twelve-satellite maritime communications constellation. Portugal's space authority ANACOM records its licensed function plainly: providing VDES - VHF Data Exchange System - and AIS service in support of maritime navigation, with global coverage, on the maritime VHF channels around 156-162 MHz. That makes it a space-based ship-reporting and two-way maritime data relay: vessel positions and messages from outside coastal VHF range, which is the gap in every coastal state's traffic picture.

POSIDONIA.organization: Govern de les Illes Balears / Open Cosmos
POSIDONIA.purpose: Posidonia is the first satellite promoted by the Balearic Islands, named for the seagrass that defines the archipelago's coastline, co-financed and operated by Open Cosmos with EU recovery funding. It flies as part of the initial deployment of OpenConstellation 1.0, a shared 15-satellite Earth-observation network whose selling point is latency - imagery turned into actionable product in as little as 30 minutes during an emergency. For the Balearics the driving cases are Mediterranean wildfires, storms and floods, and coastal and territorial management.

PRISMA (ASI hyperspectral).purpose: PRISMA - PRecursore IperSpettrale della Missione Applicativa - is ASI's hyperspectral Earth observation satellite, built by a consortium led by OHB Italia with the electro-optics from Leonardo. It pairs an imaging spectrometer covering the visible/near-infrared and shortwave infrared at 30 m ground sampling with a 5 m panchromatic camera, so a scene can be resolved geometrically and then read for the spectral signature - the chemical and physical composition - of what is in it. That combination is what makes hyperspectral data useful over water: chlorophyll and algal-bloom monitoring, water quality in inland and coastal waters, and pollution detection, as well as soil, mineral and vegetation work ashore.

PRSC-E03.purpose: EO-3, the third satellite of SUPARCO's indigenous electro-optical remote sensing constellation, joining PRSS-1 and PakTES-1A in Pakistan's Earth observation fleet. Beyond the imaging payload it carries experimental hardware: a multi-geometry imaging module, an advanced energy storage system, and an onboard AI-powered processing unit meant to do the analysis aboard the spacecraft rather than after downlink.

PRSS 1.purpose: Pakistan's first remote sensing satellite, a Chinese-built sun-synchronous spacecraft carrying an optical and electronic payload at 0.98 m panchromatic and 2.89 m multispectral resolution and a four-day revisit anywhere on the globe, controlled from ground stations at Islamabad and Karachi. SUPARCO uses the imagery for land mapping, agriculture assessment, urban and rural planning, environmental and disaster monitoring, water resource management and monitoring of China-Pakistan Economic Corridor infrastructure.

PSN N5.purpose: Satelit Nusantara Lima, a Boeing-built communications satellite delivered to PT Pasifik Satelit Nusantara in August 2025 and launched the following month, entering commercial service in early 2026. Boeing describes it as providing reliable, high-capacity connectivity across Indonesia's more than 17,000 islands and neighbouring countries. It is the largest capacity increment PSN has added and, with Nusantara Satu and Nusantara Tiga, completes a private Indonesian operator's three-satellite broadband architecture over the archipelago.

PVSAT.purpose: KARI's Performance Verification Satellite, the 180 kg payload flown on the second flight of the Nuri (KSLV-II) rocket to show the launcher could put a real satellite into its target orbit and to check Korean-built hardware - a domestically developed battery, a control moment gyro and an S-band antenna - in the space environment. It also acted as the carrier for the flight's student payloads, holding five cubesat deployers with four university cubesats and one dummy.

QB50 PRECURSOR.purpose: A QB50 precursor cubesat, flown ahead of the QB50 network to qualify its instruments and platform. QB50's premise was that the lower thermosphere between roughly 200 and 380 km is the least-measured layer of the atmosphere — too high for balloons and aircraft, too low for satellites to linger in — and that a swarm of cheap cubesats decaying through it could sample it in situ across many points at once. That region is where atmospheric drag lives, so its density and composition are exactly what orbit prediction and re-entry forecasting depend on.

QPS-SAR.organization: iQPS (Institute for Q-shu Pioneers of Space)
QPS-SAR.purpose: A QPS-SAR spacecraft, built and flown by iQPS of Fukuoka, a company founded on Kyushu University's small-satellite work. Each satellite unfurls a 3.6 m X-band radar antenna at 9.6 GHz and images in two modes, 1.8 m stripmap and 46 cm spotlight, so it works through cloud and in darkness, which is what makes small SAR the practical sensor for maritime surveillance and disaster assessment. iQPS sells the imagery commercially and is filling out a constellation intended to cut revisit over a chosen area to minutes rather than days. The catalog appends the Japanese deity nicknames iQPS gives each spacecraft: TSUKUYOMI, AMATERU, SUSANOO, WADATSUMI and others.

QUETZSAT 1.purpose: A Ku-band direct-to-home broadcasting satellite at 77 degrees West, operated within the SES fleet through QuetzSat, a joint venture between SES and Mexico's Grupo Medcom. Its 32 Ku-band transponders cover Mexico, the United States and Central America, and the capacity is fully contracted to an EchoStar subsidiary serving Dish Mexico. It is a pure broadcast asset with no government or dual-use role.

QUICK3.purpose: QUICK3 is a nanosatellite built on a Lithuanian NanoAvionics bus to fly a satellite-borne quantum light source. It has two objectives: demonstrating ultra-secure quantum communication using single-photon encoding - the basis of satellite quantum key distribution, where the physics rather than the mathematics guarantees that a key cannot be intercepted unnoticed - and testing the Born rule, a foundational principle of quantum mechanics, in microgravity for the first time.

QZS.purpose: A Michibiki satellite of Japan's Quasi-Zenith Satellite System, the regional positioning system the Cabinet Office operates to complement GPS. Most members fly the north-south asymmetric figure-of-eight quasi-zenith orbit that parks a satellite high over Japan for the greater part of each day, because a signal arriving from near the zenith is the one that urban canyons and mountains do not block; the constellation has been operated as a four-satellite system since November 2018, with three satellites always visible from the Asia-Oceania region. QZS-2 and QZS-4 are two of the quasi-zenith-orbit members. For a positioning user in the western Pacific this means more satellites at usable elevation and, through the sub-metre and centimetre-level augmentation signals the same spacecraft broadcast, better accuracy than GPS alone.

QZS-1R REPLACEMENT.purpose: QZS-1R, the replacement for the first quasi-zenith satellite. Michibiki-1 flew from 2010 as the system's pathfinder; QZS-1R took over its quasi-zenith slot in 2021, so the oldest position in the constellation is now held by an operational spacecraft carrying the full Michibiki signal set rather than a demonstrator.

QZS-3 SBAS.purpose: QZS-3, the geostationary member of the original four-satellite Michibiki constellation. Beyond positioning it carries Japan's satellite-based augmentation broadcast: since April 2020 the SBAS signal generated by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has been transmitted from a geostationary QZS rather than from the retired MTSAT spacecraft, giving aircraft range-error corrections and satellite-anomaly warnings over Japanese airspace.

QZS-6 MICHIBIKI 6.purpose: Michibiki No. 6, the first of the three satellites added to grow QZSS from four spacecraft to seven. The Cabinet Office confirmed it reached its operational geostationary position at about 90.5 degrees East in February 2025, well west of Japan, which pushes the reach of the system's signals across the Indian Ocean region rather than only over the home islands.

QZS-7 MICHIBIKI 7.purpose: Michibiki No. 7, launched on an H3 in August 2026 into a slightly inclined geosynchronous orbit. It was meant to complete the expansion of QZSS from four satellites to seven, the point of which is that at least four Michibiki satellites would then be over Japan at all times and the system could provide positioning on its own without GPS signals; the loss of Michibiki 5 in an H3 failure in December 2025 leaves that goal one spacecraft short for now.

RADARSAT 2.purpose: Canada's second-generation C-band synthetic aperture radar satellite, built, owned and operated by MDA Space with construction and launch part-funded by the Canadian Space Agency. Radar sees through cloud, fog and polar darkness, which is why the RADARSAT programme was created in the first place: the Canadian Ice Service uses it to detect ice edges, identify ice types and study ice structure using its multiple polarisation options. For maritime domain awareness, CSA notes that RADARSAT-2's 3 m Ultra-Fine beam mode improves ship detection and can help classify vessels, and the same data supports oil-spill tracking and wind and wave measurement.

RADARSAT CONSTELLATION MISSION.purpose: The RADARSAT Constellation Mission: three identical C-band SAR satellites, Canada's third generation of radar Earth observation, flown by the Canadian Space Agency for more than a dozen federal departments. Each spacecraft carries a secondary Automatic Identification System payload that receives ships' messages over a wider swath than the radar itself, so RCM fuses cooperative AIS reporting with non-cooperative radar detection - the classic way to find the vessel that is there but not squawking. CSA lists maritime surveillance, covering ice, surface wind, oil pollution and ship monitoring, as one of the mission's three design purposes, and the constellation gives daily revisit of Canada's territory and maritime approaches with Arctic access up to four times a day.

RAISE.purpose: A RAISE small demonstration satellite, the Rapid Innovative payload demonstration SatellitE series that anchors each JAXA Innovative Satellite Technology Demonstration flight. JAXA solicits component and instrument themes from Japanese industry, universities and research institutes, flies the selected ones as hosted payloads, operates the satellite to the proposers' requirements and returns both the experiment data and the environmental data recorded alongside it. It is a shared flight-heritage service rather than a mission with a science goal of its own.

RASAT.purpose: The first Earth observation satellite designed and assembled in Turkiye, built by TUBITAK UZAY as a 93 kg technology demonstrator carrying a 7.5 m panchromatic and 15 m colour imager. TUBITAK records that it was retired on 23 August 2022, so it is a decayed-mission object still catalogued rather than an active sensor. Its value was in establishing the national clean room, thermal-vacuum and vibration infrastructure and a domestic flight computer and X-band transmitter, which the later GOKTURK-2 and IMECE spacecraft inherited.

RASCOM QAF 1R.purpose: RASCOM-QAF 1R is a Thales Alenia Space Spacebus 4000B3 geostationary satellite operated by RascomStar-QAF from 2.9 degrees East. RASCOM is a multilateral organisation created in 1992 and now comprising 45 African states, formed to give the continent its own satellite telecommunications infrastructure; RascomStar-QAF is the special-purpose company set up to finance, build and operate the system. Its C- and Ku-band capacity supports pan-African television broadcasting, VSAT corporate and internet services, GSM backhaul and rural network extension. 1R was the replacement for the original RASCOM-QAF 1, which suffered a helium leak shortly after launch.

RESOURCESAT.purpose: ISRO's operational land-resources imaging line, carrying three cameras on each spacecraft: LISS-4 at 5.8 m in three visible and near-infrared bands, steerable up to plus or minus 26 degrees across track to give a five-day revisit; the medium-resolution LISS-3 with an added shortwave-infrared band; and the wide-field AWiFS. Resourcesat-2 widened the LISS-4 swath from 23 km to 70 km and improved radiometric accuracy over Resourcesat-1, and Resourcesat-2A continues the same data services to global users.

RISAT-2B SERIES.purpose: India's X-band synthetic aperture radar imaging satellites. ISRO describes them as radar imaging earth observation satellites serving agriculture, forestry and disaster management, and radar is the reason: it images through cloud, haze and darkness, so flood extent and storm damage can be mapped when an optical satellite would return a white square. The same property is what makes X-band SAR the backbone of maritime surveillance -- ship detection does not wait for a clear day -- and the RISAT series is consistently read in India as serving that end as well.

RISING 2 RAIJIN.purpose: RISING-2, a 50 kg microsatellite built jointly by Hokkaido University and Tohoku University. Its instruments are aimed at the atmosphere: a VLF receiver, a bolometer camera, a lightning and sprite imager and a high-precision telescope whose near-infrared channel uses the world's first liquid crystal tunable filter flown in space, giving configurable narrow bands between 650 and 1050 nm. The scientific target is severe convection — cumulonimbus structure and the electrical discharges above it.

ROBUSTA-3A.purpose: Robusta-3A, also called Méditerranée, is a 3U cubesat from the University of Montpellier's space centre, flown on the first Ariane 6. It carries a data-collection payload that relays measurements from ground weather stations in the Mediterranean basin — the same store-and-forward principle Argos uses — together with a radiation experiment on bipolar transistors, which is what the ROBUSTA name originally stood for.

SAOCOM.purpose: CONAE's pair of L-band synthetic aperture radar satellites, and the only operational civil L-band SAR constellation flown outside Japan. L-band penetrates vegetation canopy and the top layer of soil in a way X-band cannot, which is why SAOCOM's headline product is operational soil-moisture mapping for Argentine agriculture, hydrology and flood forecasting, alongside interferometric ground-motion work. The pair is flown as part of SIASGE, an ASI-CONAE agreement that operates them jointly with Italy's X-band COSMO-SkyMed constellation to give a two-band, twice-daily radar look for emergency management.

SARAL.purpose: A joint Indian-French oceanography mission: an ISRO bus carrying CNES instruments, principally AltiKa, the first oceanographic radar altimeter to work in Ka-band at 35.75 GHz, alongside an Argos-3 data-collection and platform-location receiver. Ka-band is far less affected by the ionosphere than the Ku-band altimeters before it and gives better vertical and spatial resolution, at the price of sensitivity to heavy rain. Altimetry is the measurement that yields sea-surface height, and from it the mesoscale eddy and current field that governs ocean routing and acoustic propagation.

SATMAR.purpose: SATMAR is a 6U nanosatellite built by the Vigo company Alen Space, funded through the Spanish ports authority's Ports 4.0 programme, to demonstrate the VHF Data Exchange System in orbit. VDES is the standard intended to succeed AIS: it keeps the AIS ship-reporting function but adds a two-way VHF data channel, so a vessel far offshore can exchange messages with a port control centre rather than only broadcasting its position. Alen Space has since run pilot campaigns in the Bay of Algeciras - ship-to-port messaging, oceanographic data relay from a drifting platform, and long-range reception of AIS from vessels well outside coastal coverage.

SAUDICOMSAT.purpose: A series of 12 kg Saudi microsatellites built at the KACST Space Research Institute for store-and-forward communications -- the satellite collects a message as it passes one station and delivers it over another, which is how low-cost spacecraft served remote users before continuous constellations existed. They were based on the SaudiSat 1 design and intended as the start of a much larger constellation that was never completed. SaudiComsat 7 additionally carried an Automatic Identification System receiver to gather ship position data from orbit, an early example of space-based AIS.

SAUDISAT 1C.purpose: The third of the first-generation SaudiSat microsatellites built by the Space Research Institute at King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology in Riyadh. The design provides store-and-forward communications and carries an amateur radio payload; this spacecraft is known to radio operators as Saudi-OSCAR 50 and has been one of the longer-lived amateur relays in low orbit.

SAUDISAT 2.purpose: A roughly 30 kg KACST experimental satellite, larger than the first-generation SaudiSats and carrying the programme's first imaging attempt: a remote sensing camera with resolution better than 15 m. It also served as a target for the Saudi Laser Station's satellite laser ranging work, which is a precision orbit determination capability in its own right.

SAUDISAT 3.purpose: A 200 kg follow-on to the earlier SaudiSat projects and much larger than them, using high resolution imagers supplied by SUNspace of South Africa together with KACST's own Space Research Institute for Earth observation. It is the point where the Saudi programme moved from amateur-scale store-and-forward payloads towards operational imaging.

SAUDISAT 4.purpose: A KACST technology demonstration satellite whose main payload is a joint NASA Ames/KACST experiment on controlling charge build-up on the free-floating test mass of a gravitational reference sensor. A GRS is an extremely accurate accelerometer that lets a spacecraft fly an orbit defined by gravity alone rather than by drag and solar pressure; charge accumulating on its test mass is one of the limits on how well it can do that, and the experiment discharged it with ultraviolet LEDs by photoemission.

SAUDISAT 5.purpose: Two 425 kg KACST Earth observation and technology demonstration satellites carrying a regionally optimised hyperspectral imaging system, launched together on a Chinese Long March 2D. They replace SaudiSat 2 and SaudiSat 3, and mark the Saudi programme's move from tens-of-kilogram experiments to operational-class imaging spacecraft.

SCATSAT 1.purpose: A dedicated scatterometer satellite flown so that the Oceansat-2 wind record would not have a gap. A scatterometer measures the roughness of the sea surface from radar backscatter and inverts it into a wind vector -- speed and direction -- across the open ocean; ISRO states the mission exists to provide wind vector data products for weather forecasting and cyclone detection and tracking. For a forecaster it is one of very few sources of surface winds where there are no ships or buoys.

SCD (INPE).purpose: The Satelite de Coleta de Dados pair, the pioneers of Brazil's environmental data collection system and the first satellites designed, built, tested and operated in Brazil. They act as orbiting relays: hundreds of automatic data collection platforms on land, on rivers and at sea transmit temperature, humidity, rainfall and pressure readings up to the spacecraft, which retransmit them to receiving stations at Cuiaba and Alcantara for distribution through INPE's SINDA system. That is a genuine METOC feed, since the buoy and river-gauge observations they carry are the in-situ backbone of Brazilian weather, hydrology and flood forecasting.

SCISAT 1.purpose: SCISAT carries the Atmospheric Chemistry Experiment, a Canadian mission led from the University of Waterloo that measures the chemistry controlling ozone in the stratosphere, with particular emphasis on the changes over Canada and the Arctic. Its two instruments, the ACE-FTS infrared Fourier transform spectrometer and the MAESTRO UV-visible-near-IR spectrophotometer, work mainly in solar occultation, returning altitude profiles of temperature, pressure and the mixing ratios of dozens of trace gases. It was the first atmospheric research satellite Canada developed and flew since ISIS-2 in the early 1970s, and it has run far beyond its planned two-year life.

SCOT-1 (SCOT).purpose: SCOT, the Space Camera for Object Tracking, is the first mission of Digantara and one of the first commercial space situational awareness satellites: rather than looking down, it looks out, tracking resident space objects from a sun-synchronous orbit to catch smaller debris at higher revisit rates than existing ground-based systems manage. The company is Indian and describes SCOT as India's first homegrown space surveillance mission, though the spacecraft is catalogued under Singapore registration. Space surveillance from orbit matters operationally because ground radar and optical networks have coverage gaps over ocean areas.

SDS-4 SPAISE.purpose: JAXA's fourth Small Demonstration Satellite, a 50 kg cube flown to prove four unrelated technologies at once. The one that mattered operationally was SPAISE, a space-based receiver for the Automatic Identification System broadcasts of ships: it tested whether AIS can be collected from orbit far out to sea and how badly reception suffers when many transmitters are in view of the same satellite at once. Japan's later radar satellites carry the operational descendants of that receiver.

SDX (SPADEX).purpose: The two SpaDeX spacecraft, flown as a pair to demonstrate rendezvous and docking in orbit. ISRO completed the docking of SDX-01 and SDX-02 on 16 January 2025, an event reported internationally as making India the fourth country to dock two spacecraft. Docking is the enabling technology behind crewed missions, space station assembly, on-orbit refuelling and satellite servicing -- none of which are possible without it, which is why a small two-satellite mission counts as a national first.

SEEDS NIHON.purpose: SEEDS-II, the Space Engineering Education Satellite of Nihon University: a 1 kg, 10 cm CubeSat rebuilt after the first SEEDS was lost in the 2006 Dnepr launch failure, and the university's first spacecraft actually to reach orbit. It transmits CW and FM telemetry on the amateur bands, and the mission is what the name says — training engineers by making them build, qualify and operate a real satellite.

SERVIS 2.organization: USEF / Japan Space Systems, for METI
SERVIS 2.purpose: The second Space Environment Reliability Verification Integrated System satellite, flown for Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. The programme exists to answer one question with real orbital data: which commercial off-the-shelf parts and design techniques survive the space environment well enough to be used in spacecraft. Its output is a parts database and design guidelines meant to cut the cost of Japanese satellites.

SES.purpose: A geostationary satellite of SES, the Luxembourg operator that flies the largest combined GEO and MEO commercial fleet — around 120 spacecraft carrying video distribution and data connectivity for broadcasters, network operators, airlines, shipping and more than sixty governments. SES describes itself as the only commercial operator running a proven medium-Earth-orbit constellation alongside a geostationary fleet, and it absorbed Intelsat in 2025, so much of the world's commercial C- and Ku-band GEO capacity now sits under one operator. For a maritime or expeditionary user this is the ordinary commercial layer that carries reachback when a military system is saturated or out of footprint.

SES AMC AMERICOM.purpose: An AMC geostationary satellite, from the GE Americom fleet that SES bought in 2001 to become SES Americom. The AMC spacecraft carry C-, Ku- and in the later models Ka-band capacity over North America for cable programming distribution, enterprise networks and government users; AMC-6 launched as GE-6 and kept both designations in the registry. They are the American half of what is now one global SES fleet.

SGDC.purpose: The Satelite Geoestacionario de Defesa e Comunicacoes Estrategicas, Brazil's dedicated defence and strategic-communications satellite, built by Thales Alenia Space and operated by the state company Telebras from operations centres sited inside military areas and staffed exclusively by Brazilians. Its Ka-band payload was conceived to carry high-speed data across the whole national territory under the national broadband plan, while its X-band payload, which Telebras puts at about 30 per cent of the satellite's capacity, is reserved for the exclusive use of the armed forces. It is the clearest South American example of a state buying assured, nationally controlled military SATCOM rather than leasing commercial capacity.

SHARJAHSAT-2.purpose: A 6U cubesat from the Sharjah Space and Astronomy Hub, integrated by ISISPACE and carrying a Simera Sense HyperScape100 hyperspectral imager. It is a municipal tool as much as a research spacecraft: the imagery is intended for urban development, infrastructure management and planning in the Emirate of Sharjah, in partnership with the emirate's electricity, water and gas authority, its municipality and its planning department.

SINAH 1.purpose: Iran's first satellite: a 160 kg experimental spacecraft built by Russia's NPO Polyot on the Sterkh bus and launched on a Kosmos-3M. Published accounts disagree about what it carried -- some describe an imaging payload, others a communications payload -- and the name is more properly Sina 1, with the catalog using a common mis-transcription. Treat the payload description as unresolved.

SINGTEL CHUNGHWA ST 2.purpose: ST-2 is a geostationary communications satellite jointly owned by Singapore Telecommunications and Taiwan's Chunghwa Telecom, launched in 2011 to replace ST-1 at 88° East. It carries C- and Ku-band capacity across South and South-East Asia, the Middle East and Australia for telecom carriers, broadcasters and maritime users, and it is one of the few operational satellites owned in common by companies from Singapore and Taiwan.

SKY MEXICO-1.purpose: A GEOStar-2 direct-to-home broadcasting satellite built by Orbital Sciences for DirecTV Latin America and stationed at 78.8 degrees West. It carries 24 active Ku-band transponders plus two R-band transponders and delivers pay-television to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. Like QuetzSat 1 it is a commercial broadcast satellite registered to Mexico but operated by a foreign platform owner.

SKY MUSTER.purpose: The two Ka-band satellites that deliver Australia's national broadband network to homes and businesses in regional and remote areas - the parts of the continent where fibre and fixed wireless will never pay. Coverage extends beyond mainland Australia and Tasmania to Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, Lord Howe Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands. They are the clearest example in this catalog of geostationary broadband deployed as public infrastructure for a low-density, very large territory.

SKYBEE.purpose: A SkyBee satellite, flown by the German company constellr to measure land surface temperature from orbit at about 30 m resolution. Thermal infrared at that scale reads the temperature of an individual field, and a plant's canopy temperature rises before any visible sign of water stress appears — which is why the primary market is irrigation and crop management, with urban heat and industrial monitoring alongside. constellr flies the visible and near-infrared bands co-registered with the thermal ones so the temperature can be attributed to what is actually on the ground.

SKYKRAFT AIR TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT.purpose: Skykraft of Canberra is building the world's first full-service space-enabled air traffic management constellation, and these are its prototype and pre-production blocks - note that the catalog spells the later batch SKYCRAFT while the earlier ones are SKYKRAFT. Each satellite carries an ADS-B receiver to capture aircraft position reports and, unusually, a VHF payload that relays controller-pilot voice and data link communications directly between aircraft using their existing radios and the air navigation service provider. Skykraft demonstrated space-based VHF with Airservices Australia in 2023 and has an ITU filing accepted for a 2976-satellite system; the practical significance is closing the surveillance and communications gap over oceanic and remote airspace, which covers most of the planet.

SNUGLITE.purpose: A 2 kg, 2U cubesat from Seoul National University flown for technology demonstration and amateur-radio work. Its central payload is an in-house dual-frequency GPS receiver being proved in orbit; paired with a boom-mounted fine magnetometer it also measures ionospheric total electron content and magnetic field, which is the quantity that drives single-frequency GNSS position error. It transmits a UHF beacon that any suitably equipped ground station can decode.

SNUSAT-2.purpose: A 3U cubesat supported by Seoul National University and built around early point-of-interest scanning for disaster monitoring: it pairs a wide-angle camera for finding the area of interest with a high-resolution camera for imaging it. The mission also flight-tests a star tracker and Earth sensor developed in-house, with telemetry on UHF and a faster S-band downlink for the imagery.

SOAP.purpose: SOAP is a space-surveillance demonstrator from the Toulouse manufacturer U-Space: it observes other objects from orbit rather than looking at the Earth, to show what space-based space situational awareness adds to the ground radar and optical networks, and specifically to improve how much small debris can be catalogued and how accurately. Observing from orbit removes the atmosphere and the day-night constraint that limit ground sensors, which is why every major space power is now flying something like it.

SOCRATES SOTA.purpose: SOCRATES, the Space Optical Communications Research Advanced Technology Satellite, flown by Japan's National Institute of Information and Communications Technology. It carried SOTA, a compact laser transponder built to show that a microsatellite can send data to the ground by light rather than radio, and to measure the real problem with that idea: the atmospheric turbulence that scintillates an optical downlink.

SORAYA.purpose: An Iranian satellite of the SRI research series, built by the Iranian Space Research Center and placed in a roughly 750 km orbit by an Iranian Qaem-100 launcher. The orbit was higher than Iran had previously reached, which is why France, Britain, Germany and the United States responded to the launch primarily as a demonstration of long-range rocket technology. No payload performance has been published.

SPACEEYE-T1.purpose: SpaceEye-T is the first satellite Satrec Initiative owns and operates for itself rather than building for a government customer, and the opening piece of a privately owned Korean very-high-resolution constellation. Its EOS-T imager works in one panchromatic and four multispectral bands, resolving 0.25 m panchromatic and 1 m multispectral over a 12 km swath. That is fine enough for port and vessel-scale detail, and the mission is catalogued for ocean imagery as well as land.

SPACEVAN.purpose: A spacevan orbital transfer vehicle, flown by the French company Exotrail. Like D-Orbit's ION carriers these are tugs rather than free-flyers: a rideshare launch drops everything into one orbit, and the spacevan then uses electric propulsion to move customer satellites to the orbit they actually wanted before releasing them, a service the industry calls last-mile delivery. spacevan-001 made Exotrail's first such delivery on 28 February 2024, releasing the 8U cubesat EXO-0. So the honest answer to "what is this satellite" is that it is a vehicle carrying other people's satellites, and what it is doing depends on whose payload is aboard.

SPARTAN (EnduroSat).purpose: SPARTAN - Shared Platform for Applied Research and Technology AffirmatioN - is a 6U CubeSat flown by the Bulgarian manufacturer EnduroSat as a shared ride for payloads rather than a single-purpose mission, carrying seven separate payloads on one bus. Shared-satellite missions of this kind are how small developers buy flight heritage for a component without funding a whole spacecraft.

SPEQTRE.purpose: A CubeSat quantum key distribution demonstrator led by the UK's RAL Space with the Singaporean company SpeQtral, flying on an ISISPACE platform. The mission tests the exchange of quantum-encoded key material from a spacecraft roughly the size of a microwave oven, aiming at communications where any interception attempt is detectable as a matter of physics and which remain secure against future quantum computers. It is a technology risk-reduction flight for satellite QKD, not an operational secure link.

SPRINT A HISAKI.purpose: Hisaki, the first spacecraft dedicated to observing the planets from Earth orbit. Its extreme-ultraviolet spectroscope watched Venus, Mars and Jupiter continuously for far longer stretches than a fly-by allows, to study how the atmospheres of the terrestrial planets escape to space and how Jupiter's magnetosphere is driven. It was the first mission of JAXA's small scientific satellite series and was deactivated in December 2023.

SRMSAT.purpose: A student-built nanosatellite from SRM University, Chennai, developed under ISRO's technical guidance. Its payload is a grating spectrometer for monitoring greenhouse gases in the near infrared between roughly 900 and 1700 nm -- an atmospheric composition instrument on an 8.5 kg spacecraft, and a working demonstration that a university team can fly real remote sensing rather than just a beacon.

SSOT.purpose: Also called FASat-Charlie, the spacecraft of Chile's Sistema Satelital de Observacion Terrestre, operated by the Chilean Air Force and the first fully autonomous national imaging capability the Chilean state has held. The air force describes it as designed to deliver high-resolution imagery supporting civil, scientific and defence decision-making, and it has supplied strategic information to the armed services as well as mapping and disaster response products. It is the standard example of a small state fielding a single dual-use optical satellite under military operation.

SSTL S1-4.purpose: A 440 kg SSTL high-resolution optical satellite carrying an SSTL-designed imager that returns sub-metre panchromatic and sub-4-metre multispectral imagery over a swath of about 20.8 km. Its 45-degree off-pointing agility and spot, strip and mosaic modes let it acquire several separated targets in a single pass. Imaging capacity is leased to Airbus, to 21AT and to LatConnect60.

STAR ONE (EMBRATEL).purpose: Embratel's Star One fleet, the main Brazilian-owned commercial geostationary capacity, controlled from the Guaratiba teleport in Rio de Janeiro and serving television distribution, telephony backhaul, corporate data and internet across Brazil and South America. Star One C2 works 65 degrees West with C, Ku and X-band transponders and coverage extending to Mexico and Florida; the C3, C4 and D1 spacecraft carry the third and fourth generations; Star One D2 is the largest of the fleet with C, Ku, Ka and X-band payloads. The X-band capacity on C2 and D2 is the detail worth noting, since X-band is the band allied navies use for protected satellite communications.

STEP CUBE LAB-II.purpose: A 6U cubesat developed at Chosun University in Gwangju and deployed from PVSAT on Nuri's second flight. It carries an electro-optical camera together with mid-wave and long-wave infrared cameras and its own image processing and transmission chain, flying Korea's first multiband infrared Earth-observation mission from a cubesat. High-damping laminated solar panels, pogo-pin restraints and a panel drive mechanism are being tested in orbit alongside the cameras.

STRAND 1.purpose: The world's first phonesat and the first UK CubeSat launched: a 3U nanosatellite built largely in engineers' own time by the University of Surrey's Surrey Space Centre with SSTL, carrying a Google Nexus One smartphone running Android as an experimental onboard computer. It also flew two novel propulsion systems - eight pulsed plasma thrusters and a water-alcohol resistojet - plus what is believed to be the first 3D-printed part in orbit. Antenna problems meant the smartphone could never be run long enough to take over satellite operations.

STRIX.purpose: A StriX small radar satellite operated by Synspective of Tokyo. The design came out of Japan's government-funded ImPACT programme and was developed jointly with the University of Tokyo, the Tokyo Institute of Technology and JAXA; a foldable antenna, more power and aggressive use of commercial parts let a small, cheap bus return imagery comparable to far larger SAR spacecraft. Synspective sells the data for ground-displacement and infrastructure monitoring and for disaster response, and because radar sees through cloud and at night the same satellites support persistent coastal and maritime observation.

STSAT 3.organization: KARI / KAIST SaTReC / Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute
STSAT 3.purpose: The third Science and Technology Satellite, a 170 kg mission for space observation and technology verification. Its main payload MIRIS, from the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, is a near-infrared imaging system that observes both the sky and the Earth - surveying the cosmic infrared background and the Paschen-alpha line along the Galactic plane - while the secondary COMIS compact imaging spectrometer monitors changes in the Earth environment. It also served as the flight test for a Hall thruster, lithium-ion batteries and a composite multi-functional structure.

STUTTGART FLYING LAPTOP.purpose: Flying Laptop is a small satellite designed, built, tested and operated by students and staff at the University of Stuttgart's Institute of Space Systems, carrying a multispectral imager, an AIS ship-tracking receiver and a set of technology experiments. It is one of the more capable university-built spacecraft in Europe and has served as an in-orbit testbed for hardware that later flew on other missions.

SUPERBIRD.purpose: A Superbird geostationary communications satellite of SKY Perfect JSAT, built by Mitsubishi Electric on the Japanese DS2000 bus. Superbird-C2, catalogued here as SUPERBIRD 7, replaced Superbird-C and covers the Asia-Pacific region, the Indian Ocean, Oceania and the Pacific islands as well as Japan itself, which puts commercial Ku-band capacity across most of the western Pacific operating area.
